# 11. Generative methods

Chapters 9 and 10 ask what a roguelike should generate: levels, items, monsters, text. This chapter is about how. It covers the machinery under every generator, from weighted lists, seeds and noise through wave function collapse, constraint solvers, grammars and Markov chains to optimisers, simulated players and language models, and the work around that machinery: deciding whether to generate at all, making the output perceptibly varied, proving it playable, seeing what the generator actually makes, and keeping a person in the loop. It matters because the generator is where a roguelike's runs come from, and so where samey runs, unwinnable seeds and text that falls apart come from too.

The talks approach the subject from many directions: developers explaining shipped systems, researchers presenting formal tools, and artists, musicians and poets borrowing structure from outside games. Their common thread is that a generator is encoded design knowledge, not free content. What makes one good is how its output is shaped, checked and selected, not how much it can produce.

## In brief

- Decide what a generator should do for the player before you pick a technique, and choose generative systems like materials, by the experience you want rather than by what the technology offers ([Isaac Karth 2019, 0:08](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=8); [Gillian Smith 2026, 1:14:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4472); [Alexei Pepers 2019, 3:36](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=216); [Bruno Dias 2016, 17:53](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=1073)).
- Do not generate to save work: tuning a generator is a different skill, not an easier one, and its real cost is the design knowledge you have to encode in it ([Brian Walker 2018, 2:15](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=135); [Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:03:00](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=3780); [Younès Rabii 2025, 17:05](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1025); [Younès Rabii 2025, 4:45](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=285)).
- Unique is not the same as interesting: many talks independently warn that a generator can produce endless outputs players cannot tell apart, so aim for differences players perceive in play ([Isaac Karth 2019, 8:29](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=509); [Pierre Vigier 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=720); [Darius Kazemi 2017, 10:17](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=617); [Cole Wehrle 2025, 16:01](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=961); [Younès Rabii 2025, 22:55](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1375); [Isaac Karth 2019, 18:34](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1114)).
- Treat randomness as an input to an algorithm that carries your intent, and shape it with weights, curves, overdue-event boosts and causal links instead of flat rolls ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 3:50](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=230); [Tyler Coleman 2024, 28:00](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1680); [Nifflas 2025, 6:03](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=363); [Alex Byaly 2022, 15:16](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=916)).
- Derive random values from a hash of the situation and a master seed, with one sub-generator per aspect of the world, so any place can be generated in any order and any player's bug can be reproduced ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 0:46](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=46); [Andrew Clifton 2020, 6:05](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=365); [Alexander Birke 2024, 2:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=160); [Alexander Birke 2024, 3:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=220); [Alexander Birke 2024, 4:02](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=242)).
- Example-based methods such as wave function collapse produce texture cheaply from a tiny drawn sample, but they only know local similarity, so wrap them in higher-level structure or a play-derived skeleton when the level needs global properties ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 4:33](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=273); [Brian Bucklew 2019, 15:30](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=930); [Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 47:40](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2860); [Emily Halina 2024, 22:26](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1346); [Emily Halina 2024, 23:18](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1398)).
- Guide your randomness and then check the result: guarantee anything that blocks progress, such as reachable stairs or a key outside its own door, and let optional content fail occasionally ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:35](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1475); [Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804); [Stella Mazeika 2019, 6:53](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=413)).
- Look at a generator in bulk before judging it: expressive range analysis (score many outputs on game-specific metrics and plot them) is the closest thing the talks have to standard practice, and its outliers and clusters tell you which outputs to inspect by hand ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:44](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=164); [Various 2018, 2:22](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=142); [Oliver Withington 2024, 7:41](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=461); [Oliver Withington 2024, 12:50](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=770); [Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 5:04](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=304)).
- A solver or simple player model can teach you a lot about generated content: its path through a puzzle or level helps you assess difficulty, consistency and interest ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 29:02](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1742); [Jack Schlesinger 2022, 21:42](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1302); [Jack Schlesinger 2022, 28:07](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1687); [droqen 2026, 24:56](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1496)).
- Most memorable generated content had a human selecting it, so keep a designer, curator or player between the generator and the audience, and never pipe a language model's raw output to players ([Ben Berman 2017, 35:16](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2116); [Martin Pichlmair 2026, 14:54](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=894); [Gabriel Koenig 2020, 13:15](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=795); [Nat Alison 2023, 24:43](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1483); [Robin Sloan 2019, 11:21](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=681); [Janelle Shane 2022, 21:25](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1285)).

## Deciding to generate: what procgen is for

### Start with the effect, not the technique

Before choosing an algorithm, ask the question Isaac Karth puts at the centre of his vocabulary for procedural generation: why do you want to generate this particular thing, and what do you hope it does to the player? Karth calls the study of generators by the effect they create in the player "procedural generation poetics", and he proposes a set of critical lenses, each a theory that raises its own questions about a generator without claiming to be the only view ([Isaac Karth 2019, 0:08](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=8)). Gillian Smith reaches the same place from teaching: treat generative systems as materials, like paints, each with affordances, constraints and embedded ethics, and choose among them by the experience you want rather than letting the technology lead ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:14:32](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4472)).

The reason to ask first is that generation is not a neutral default. Alexei Pepers compares procedural generation to fantasy magic: people talk about its power and rarely about its downsides. You would not ask a wizard to fix your fence, because it might become sentient or turn blue, and a generator can likewise do unexpected and very bad things, especially in a newcomer's hands ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 3:36](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=216)).

> Just because Proc Gen is very powerful does not mean it should be used to solve every problem. — [Alexei Pepers 2019, 3:36](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=216)

### Generation has to be part of the design

Two talks argue that generated content only works inside a design built for it. Bruno Dias, writing procedural text for Voyageur, concludes that you cannot swap authored content for procedural content and expect it to work: both the systems and the writing style must be shaped around generation, and procgen must be demystified, taken "out of the grimoire and into the toolbox" ([Bruno Dias 2016, 17:53](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=1073)). Darius Kazemi makes the complementary point from the other side: a game's rules are the context that makes its generated content mean anything. Spelunky's level generator is lifeless on its own and becomes interesting only when you run and jump through its levels; give the game floaty controls or a different jump height and the same levels stop working as levels ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 20:38](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1238)). A good level generator cannot rescue bad movement.

### The visibility problem

A generator that the player never perceives adds little. Gabriel Koenig learned this after releasing Jettomero. Many players play once and stop, and for them a procedurally generated game is indistinguishable from a handmade one; he could have built every element by hand and most players would have had a nearly identical experience ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 5:04](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=304)). Jettomero used physics and raycasts to place objects, generated colour palettes, procedural ragdoll animation and monsters assembled from parts. Those systems made development exciting for him, but because they ran entirely behind the scenes the play experience gained almost nothing from them, and he estimates the game would have taken about the same time to make manually. The feature that best showed the generation off was the photo mode, which sat outside the gameplay ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:03:00](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=3780)). If you generate something, decide where the player will see the difference, and whether they will play enough times to see it.

### Lower the barrier: procgen can be small

None of this means generation has to be grand. Xalavier Nelson Jr. long assumed procgen was for people simulating universes until he split the word into "procedure" (according to rules) and "generation" (making stuff); by that definition, picking items from lists is as legitimate a route to lots of weird content as deep simulation ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 4:31](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=271)). He also reframes the work as making modular pieces that combine into a whole, the windows, doors and garage of a house rather than the house in a day, which is how even Dwarf Fortress's intimidating scope was built up ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2020, 5:48](https://youtu.be/SjttI9N9KSM?t=348)). Martin Pichlmair draws the same lesson from history: dice and turning wheels forced pre-digital procedural systems to stay lightweight, whereas computers make it easy to build generators that are too complicated, and we have lost the habit of straightforward design ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 24:12](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1452)).

The motive for generating has also shifted. Todd Furmanski recalls that procedural generation began as a way to save memory, as in an early Atari game that used a random number generator in about 128 bytes to produce 256 screens; today the motive is that worlds such as simulated cities and galaxies are too large to author by hand ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 0:45](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=45)).

Whatever the motive, do not expect it to save you work. Brian Walker describes procedural level design as a different skill, not an easier one: instead of laying out elements like an artist on a canvas, you build systems, generate, judge which output feels better, and tweak hyperparameters, in Brogue's case for years. He says it is not a time-saver, and that most of Brogue's development time went into tuning level generation ([Brian Walker 2018, 2:15](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=135)).

## What a generator is: possibility space, cost and encoded knowledge

### Possibility space and generative space

The rest of this chapter needs two terms that are easy to blur. Oliver Withington distinguishes the **possibility space**, everything representable in a generator's encoding, from the **generative space**, what the generator actually produces. Minecraft's possibility space is anything expressible in its voxels, including player builds its terrain generator never makes; its generative space is what that generator outputs; anything needing a block that does not exist lies outside both. Tuning a generator means moving the generative space so it sits over the good levels, narratives or weapons you want ([Oliver Withington 2024, 3:49](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=229)). Younès Rabii gives the formal version: a generator is a deterministic function from a seed to an artifact, both fixed-size binary strings, characterised by its possibility space (of scale N) and its probability distribution over it. A 1d6 generator has six equally likely outputs; 2d6 has eleven outputs with unequal odds, since many combinations make 7 and only one makes 2 ([Younès Rabii 2025, 10:43](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=643)).

Gillian Smith frames what the designer is doing with that space: procedural generation means designing an acceptable space of potential experiences rather than one perfectly crafted experience, and that space must feel unified even though no two players take the same path. Thinking in spaces lets players discover the space's odd corners themselves, and even help extend and curate it ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:08:06](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4086)). Everest Pipkin describes the work of building such a space as curation, like assembling an art show, a playlist or a book of poems: learn the ethos of the space, know what is right, then encode that as rules that find the bounded edges of an interesting possibility space and reliably produce that kind of result ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=1064)).

> To work with generative systems is to be a curator. — [Everest Pipkin 2019, 17:44](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=1064)

### Rabii's thermodynamics of generators

Rabii's formalism gives the chapter a way to talk about structure, noise and cost with some precision.

- **Complexity of an artifact.** Kolmogorov complexity is the minimum description needed to reproduce an artifact. Rabii compares three 6x6 pixel images coded in PICO-8 Lua: a checkerboard takes about 30 bytes, a flower about 60, and a noisy image has to list every pixel. Low complexity means repetitive, easy-to-spot patterns; high means noise; the in-between is often the most interesting. Exact values are almost impossible to compute but can be estimated ([Younès Rabii 2025, 14:54](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=894)).
- **Temperature.** A generator's temperature is the average complexity of its outputs: low means structured, high means noisy. A library that returns one of N stored artifacts at random is itself a generator of size N × T bits, which yields an analogue of the ideal gas law, pressure × volume = scale × temperature, and lets the bounds between these variables be plotted ([Younès Rabii 2025, 18:00](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1080)).
- **States of matter.** On that plot, solid generators are rigid, reliable, repetitive and cheap, and suit hand-made content; gaseous ones lean on random functions and are cheap and unpredictable, always looking different but perhaps not feeling different; liquid generators contain a lot of knowledge and can take distinctly different shapes through tunable parameters, as water takes its container's shape ([Younès Rabii 2025, 24:22](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1462)).

### A generator's real cost is the knowledge it encodes

Rabii's central claim follows from this. Code can always be padded with long names or dead code, but compress it to the limit and what remains is the crucial information; he calls that residue the generator's minimum information volume and reads it as the designer's knowledge encoded in the algorithm. That knowledge is what the generator really costs, in research, specification, testing and debugging ([Younès Rabii 2025, 17:05](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1025)). So generators are not free content: practitioners have long known that breadth trades off against depth and quality, which is missing from industry claims that procedural generation and generative AI make content cheaply ([Younès Rabii 2025, 4:45](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=285)).

His image for this is Maxwell's demon, the thought-experiment creature whose sorting of molecules has a hidden memory cost. A generator's separation of desirable from undesirable artifacts likewise depends on hidden human knowledge work. Generation only looks cheap if that work is ignored or taken, as when scraped datasets or underpaid labelling are treated as free. Rabii casts roguelike makers as the demons, gardeners and sculptors who know the work is not cheap ([Younès Rabii 2025, 32:08](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1928)).

### Spaces players imagine, and spaces too big to learn

The space players experience is not exactly the generator's. Cole Wehrle, discussing Oath, adds two regions to it: unseen possibilities, which the game could produce but did not, and imagined impossibilities, which players believe might happen but never can. His children invented Minecraft biomes they had heard about on the playground; both regions are part of the game ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 6:58](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=418)).

Size matters too. Paul Hembree's rhythm generator shows how a space can be small enough to learn and love, or explode past human knowledge with one small change. With sixteenth notes in 4/4 there are 431 rotations starting on notes (862 counting rests), which a dedicated person could learn in days; at thirty-second notes there are about 7,000, too many to know without statistical methods ([Paul Hembree 2026, 16:48](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1008)).

The practical consequence: budget for the knowledge you will have to encode, since that, not the code, is the cost. And be clear which space you are adjusting when you tune, the possibility space your representation allows or the generative space your rules actually reach ([Oliver Withington 2024, 3:49](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=229)).

## The oatmeal problem: variety players can actually perceive

### Unique is not the same as interesting

The most consistent warning in these talks is that a generator can produce endless distinct outputs that nobody can tell apart. Kate Compton's name for it, the "10,000 bowls of oatmeal" problem, is relayed by several speakers: Isaac Karth describes generators whose numbers differ but whose outputs blur into mush ([Isaac Karth 2019, 8:29](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=509)); Pierre Vigier finds his constraint-based room generator yields rooms that are technically different but look alike from the same input ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=720)); Todd Furmanski designs Forska's variety specifically against it ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 14:30](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=870)). Darius Kazemi makes the point without the metaphor: trivial code can generate more unique content than anyone could consume, and Markov text or Perlin-noise landscapes look good at a glance but bore within about ten seconds ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 10:17](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=617)).

The same finding turns up in other media. Cole Wehrle notes that every well-shuffled deck is a unique arrangement, yet one random deck feels like another, like one frame of static compared with another; this is why Oath's expansion keeps unused sites in order instead of reshuffling them ([Cole Wehrle 2025, 16:01](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=961)). Sonat Uzun found that random combinations of motifs and context produced many Tea Garden songs that sounded alike, so he had to engineer variation deliberately, adding mechanisms such as a shift motif ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 18:53](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1133)). Rabii's formalism explains the convergence: raise a generator's scale or output complexity without adding designer knowledge and it drifts toward a white-noise generator, which is oatmeal ([Younès Rabii 2025, 22:55](https://youtu.be/BJ_84d7v3K4?t=1375)).

> One random deck feels like another random deck. — [Cole Wehrle 2025, 16:01](https://youtu.be/HgnvMBVKP0M?t=961)

### Levels of difference

Ada Null, drawing on Compton, gives a scale for how different outputs feel. **Oatmeal** is unique but perceived as identical, like a topiary garden of identically clipped trees. **Perceptual differentiation** is clearly different but not memorable, like a forest of one wild species. **Perceptual uniqueness** is characterfully distinct, like Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, and is what most generators aim for: the output players discuss as a one-in-a-million run ([Ada Null 2025, 4:32](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=272)). The scale is a design choice, not a ladder you must climb. Kiss Garden deliberately aims for differentiation while falling short of uniqueness: walking through differentiated trees you know you are not going in circles, yet it is all the same, and that produces the ennui the game is about ([Ada Null 2025, 5:36](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=336)).

### What makes output interesting

Nat Alison proposes three criteria for compelling procedurality: complexity from simple rules, a balance of order and chaos, and surprise and joy ([Nat Alison 2024, 2:24](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=144)). On the second, complete symmetry is boring and complete randomness intractable; between a uniform grid and white noise sits Perlin noise, which feels naturalistic, and the near-patterns of the primes keep people searching for structure ([Nat Alison 2024, 12:38](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=758)). On the third, procgen succeeds best when it produces surprisingly poignant, beautiful or funny results, like the Slay the Spire moment when a synergy makes it feel as though the stars are aligning and you are somehow cheating ([Nat Alison 2024, 18:23](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=1103)).

Tyler Coleman adds who does the noticing. Players talk about a generator's artifacts, not the generator, and specifically about the outliers: among 10,000 bowls of alphabet soup, the one that spells something is the one people discuss. Build systems where the right combination of random rolls can produce rare weird results ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 23:51](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1431)). Kazemi's preference points the same way: he would rather have a Perlin landscape with a big flat rectangle dropped into it than another pleasant, plausible one ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 10:17](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=617)).

### Techniques for perceptible variety

- **Layer many small decisions.** Kazemi describes Spelunky's input as layers of probabilistic tiles: no single decision is complex, but the combinations explode ([Darius Kazemi 2017, 19:00](https://youtu.be/CLi4PWxDmAI?t=1140)).
- **Multiply independent categories.** Furmanski gets more variety per unit of work in Forska by crossing independent axes, such as four geology types times four island shapes ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 14:30](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=870)).
- **Vary the context and the inputs.** Vigier's fixes for samey rooms: vary room shape, wall textures and object skins; do not overuse one template, especially for neighbouring rooms; offer many alternative and optional objects; and let a higher-level generator produce inputs that carry meaning ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 12:00](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=720)).
- **Engineer variation where combination is not enough.** Uzun's shift motif exists because random combination alone produced similar songs ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 18:53](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1133)).

### Karth's diagnostic lenses

Karth's lenses help you find out why a generator feels flat.

- **Invariants.** What a generator never varies is often its most characteristic trait. A default NetHack level has one up and one down staircase, so when that breaks, players know something is going on ([Isaac Karth 2019, 8:00](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=480)).
- **Repetition.** Do elements repeat exactly, or resemble each other while staying unique? Not everything must stand out: Emily Short's "mushroom" content, ordinary room layouts or Markov text that matters little individually, forms a useful background carpet of generativity ([Isaac Karth 2019, 17:07](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1027)).
- **Style.** How well does each artifact fit the context it was generated for? Is the generator smart enough to put a water monster on the swamp level ([Isaac Karth 2019, 20:45](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1245))?
- **Framing.** How a generator is presented in context and described to the player shapes what players perceive it to have made ([Isaac Karth 2019, 9:20](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=560)).
- **Multiplicity players can see.** Elite Dangerous generated widely varied space station shapes, but docking required identical docking ports, so players always saw nearly the same thing. Variety the player does not perceive in play does not count ([Isaac Karth 2019, 18:34](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1114)).

### The trouble with infinity

Linas Gabrielaitis turns the problem on the promise of infinite worlds. Starbound's planets are constrained (ocean on the left, lava at the bottom), and No Man's Sky would by one calculation take 600,000 years to explore; like the Library of Babel, an infinity without meaning leaves the visitor lost ([Linas Gabrielaitis 2023, 8:57](https://youtu.be/jvZb9WoIHxo?t=537)). The practical aim, then, is not more outputs but memorable differences: decide which level on Null's scale you want, give the player axes of variation they will notice during play, keep some invariants so breaks in them mean something, and make sure the rare outlier is possible.

## Shaping randomness: distributions, weights and causal structure

### Randomness is an input, not the design

Herbert Wolverson draws a principle from Rogue and Dwarf Fortress: in good procedural games the randomness does not define the game. It feeds an algorithm that produces something approximating what the designer wants, different every time ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 3:50](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=230)). Most of the craft is in that algorithm, and much of it is about replacing flat, uniform rolls with distributions that carry intent.

### Making randomness non-uniform

Tyler Coleman's rule is "never roll alone": combine several random values, or take a uniform 0-to-1 random and pass it through an easing curve, so you get a weighted distribution instead of a flat one. He uses curved randoms in many of his games, and suggests weighting barks so a special NPC line appears only a limited number of times ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 28:00](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1680)).

Nifflas, generating music, found uniform computer randomness sounds like evenly spread white noise ([Nifflas 2025, 14:04](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=844)). Three of his devices show other ways to shape it:

- **Desire bars.** Each possible note has a desire bar that grows over time, so events that have not happened for a while become more likely. He can also control when desires are active and building, producing alternating dense and sparse phases ([Nifflas 2025, 6:03](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=363)).
- **Human-made sequences.** He drove an instrument with number sequences people invented "randomly" in their heads. Their biases, such as repeated 7s, one huge number and a single negative, gave each person's sequence a distinctive melody ([Nifflas 2025, 14:04](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=844)).
- **Crowd-voted weights.** For a drum instrument, followers voted in polls on each step of a loop, and the averaged results became the probability arrays the device samples from ([Nifflas 2025, 10:52](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=652)).

When a choice depends on several considerations at once, score it. Jurie Horneman describes dynamic location picking that rates each candidate on several metrics (suitability, recency, distance), combines them with weights into one total, and takes the top scorer or a random pick from the top few. Recency and proximity only exist at runtime, so static data analysis cannot check them, but because the per-candidate values exist they are cheap to print to a log or debug window to see why a choice was made ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 17:50](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1070)).

Weights can also ramp over a game. Todd Furmanski's Dragon's Descent for the Atari 2600 keeps noise tables in ROM, like a pre-baked noise texture, that index ten room types; raising the index range produces more ornate and dangerous rooms with lethal walls, giving him control over room complexity across levels ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=485)).

### Causal graphs

Alex Byaly's causal graphs make correlated attributes easy to generate. Think of each attribute as a raffle. Roll the cause first, then add or remove raffle tickets for the effect according to the result: roll a character's city, then adjust the weights of crimes in that city. In his demo, drawing Cliffside adds tickets for slander and tax evasion, Megalopolis for copyright infringement, Agraria for slander. Each city ends up with a distinct crime profile, and the reverse relationship, which city a given crime tends to come from, emerges for free ([Alex Byaly 2022, 15:16](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=916)).

Byaly points out why this is forgiving. Scientists struggle to build models from data because many different causal graphs fit the same data; going from graph to data, that ambiguity frees you to draw arrows in whichever direction is convenient and still get similar-looking results ([Alex Byaly 2022, 14:45](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=885)).

Two cautions. First, the raffles must be run in an order that never goes backwards along an arrow. Byaly orders species, city, food, job, crime; a loop such as species to city to food back to species cannot be honoured in a single pass, and while multiple passes might allow backward arrows, he did not try it ([Alex Byaly 2022, 17:53](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1073)). Second, chained adjustments can compound into extreme quirks: after several arrows were added, Agraria ended up almost unpopulated. You correct this by raising the base tickets or adjusting the tables ([Alex Byaly 2022, 19:56](https://youtu.be/otEv5dh2f4E?t=1196)).

### Fixed structure, free variation, a designed ending

Two talks from music offer a model for combining authored structure with chance. Matt Carney holds up Terry Riley's In C: 53 fixed melodic patterns played in order, with each performer free to choose how many times to repeat each pattern before moving on ([Matt Carney 2026, 10:17](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=617)). One simple proximity rule bounds the space: performers stay within two or three patterns of each other, keeping the piece open without letting it drift apart ([Matt Carney 2026, 11:03](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=663)). And the ending is designed: everyone waits on the last pattern until the whole ensemble arrives, the group swells and fades a few times, and players drop out at will. Carney presents this as knowing where to put your thumb on the scale to get a desired outcome while keeping agency even at the end ([Matt Carney 2026, 11:48](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=708)).

Sonat Uzun reached the same arrangement in Tea Garden. Its song structures, brief descriptions of which part enters when, are hand-written rather than random, because if enough other elements are random (each song follows a random chord progression) every song still feels different ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 23:09](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1389)). You do not have to randomise everything.

### Two kinds of randomness

Not all randomness does the same job. In Q&A at Shawn Main's talk, an audience member observed that removing either kind from a roguelike tends to turn it into a puzzle game: a fixed setup with random results, or a random setup with deterministic results such as a static five damage to a monster. Main said he had not thought of it that way ([Shawn Main 2017, 20:29](https://youtu.be/UZ7XqQYDM7o?t=1229)). Before you shape a distribution, know whether it governs what the player is handed or what happens when they act.

## Seeds, hashes and timing: when content comes into being

Two linked decisions sit under every generator: where its randomness comes from, and at what moment content is created. The first decides whether you can reproduce a world; the second decides what the world can know about itself.

### Don't generate, hash

Andrew Clifton traces a familiar progression: from one global `rand()`, to separate random number generator (RNG) instances for monster AI, dungeon generation and combat, and finally, taken to the extreme, a fresh RNG seeded per decision and drawn once. That last step is just a poor hash function. Instead, hash the information that uniquely identifies the situation and use the hash as the random value. A hash is a pure function whose outputs look uniformly random, so it can replace RNG calls and makes testing and debugging easier ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 0:46](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=46)).

What goes into the hash matters. It must uniquely identify the situation without being over-specific. For a gold pile, hashing only the coordinates would put or omit gold at the same spot on every level; add the dungeon level to fix that, and the game seed so that not every game is identical. Leave the seed out only when you want something identical across all games. Then compare the result to a threshold, say a 10% chance of a pile ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 6:05](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=365)).

When one situation needs several values (whether an object exists, its type, its attributes), Clifton combines hashing with SplitMix64. SplitMix64's state update is just adding a stream constant, gamma, which acts as a stream id (good values must be chosen carefully); all the randomness comes from a mixing finaliser. So jumping i steps is state + i × gamma, which works for negative i too and lets you run the generator backwards ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 9:26](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=566)). Hash to a seed, then pull values at different indexes: given seed, stream id and index, you get the value at that position, with no state at all ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 10:06](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=606)). Clifton is relaxed about small statistical flaws such as the low-end bias from reducing a value with modulo: he has never noticed an in-game effect, so for games he does not worry about it ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 7:32](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=452)).

Alexander Birke reaches a similar design in Sea of Rifts. He uses stateless hash and noise functions instead of traditional RNGs because the same input always yields the same value, which makes them thread-safe, easy to port to the GPU and easy to extend to more dimensions; he says he sees no use case left for traditional RNGs ([Alexander Birke 2024, 2:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=160)). He insists on determinism for a commercial reason: when you generate a whole world, narrative and cast, bugs will happen, and if you cannot recreate the player's game state you cannot find what went wrong ([Alexander Birke 2024, 3:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=220)). To keep that determinism maintainable, he "layer-cakes" generation into one generator per aspect, all seeded from a master world seed held by the world generator. Each has a clear responsibility, like composition in object-oriented code, so a generator can be tweaked or added, whether a cell generator or an abstract one such as names, without changing the others' output ([Alexander Birke 2024, 4:02](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=242)).

A seed can come from anywhere. bleeptrack's NFC sticker project uses each tag's unique ID as the colour and shape seed for a generative series and its scan counter to shuffle shapes, so every tap adds a new piece to the series ([bleeptrack 2025, 6:51](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=411)).

### When does content come into being?

At the 2016 lightning talks, Tariq of Catacomb Kids set out the range of answers as an open question. At one end, Dwarf Fortress simulates an entire world history up front; at the other, you generate the next room when the player enters it, or treat an NPC as not existing until the player talks to them ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:43](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=163)).

**Generate on entry.** Sea of Rifts keeps initial world generation short and generates most data when the player enters a cell, which eases iteration. Birke wants to jump to any point in the world for debugging and play, and that rules out solvers like wave function collapse, which grow outward from an initial state ([Alexander Birke 2024, 5:36](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=336)). Stateless hashing is what makes per-cell, arbitrary-order generation possible.

**Generate lazily, but describe ahead.** Generating late creates a problem if the game wants to refer to things that do not exist yet. Mark Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum generates its huge world only as needed, for performance and memory, but keeps detailed abstract descriptions of every future feature: the game already knows that a cathedral with certain properties will exist in a certain district. Clues can then reference that abstract description, and when the player arrives the generated cathedral matches, as if it had always been there ([Mark Johnson 2023, 22:10](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1330)).

**Generate just in time, like a game master.** Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans go further and treat generation as live orchestration, the way a tabletop game master improvises: reseed dangers, enemies and clues according to what the player actually does. Dormans's simple example is Zelda raising the chance of hearts from broken pots when health is low, or arrows when arrows are low ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 21:48](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1308)). Content whose source is a creature or an off-screen event suits this. Bane's light-attracted flutter moths, which start fires, can plausibly appear even in a room already visited, so the game can add them whenever it judges there has not been enough action; falling rocks that disturb spores can be dropped off camera via a level-specific encounter table ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 27:01](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1621)).

**Generate across time instead of space.** Max Kreminski contrasts two modes. Mining games such as Minecraft distribute generated content across space and generate on demand, so players hunt through many chunks for rare far-flung dungeons. Gardening games such as Animal Crossing distribute it across time and generate on a clock tied to the real calendar, which stops players churning through content as fast as they can click ([Max Kreminski 2018, 19:31](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=1171)). Gardening games also use many small, largely independent processes acting on one shared artifact (weeds appearing, which bugs and fish show up on which days, villagers moving in and out) rather than one large visible generator producing disposable artifacts ([Max Kreminski 2018, 18:17](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=1097)).

### Choosing a scheme

- If you need to reproduce player bugs or visit any location in any order, derive every random value from a hash of the situation plus a master seed, and give each aspect of the world its own sub-generator ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 6:05](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=365); [Alexander Birke 2024, 3:40](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=220); [Alexander Birke 2024, 4:02](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=242)).
- If generated text or clues must refer to places that do not exist yet, keep an abstract description of them from the start ([Mark Johnson 2023, 22:10](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1330)).
- If you want the game to respond to how the player is doing, leave room for just-in-time content whose appearance is plausible in the fiction ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 21:48](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1308); [Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 27:01](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1621)).
- If you want content to pace itself, consider distributing it across time rather than space ([Max Kreminski 2018, 19:31](https://youtu.be/TvlZinAvpwg?t=1171)).

## Building blocks for terrain and space: noise, cells, distance and geometry

### Noise

Perlin and Simplex noise give smooth, continuous values that are deterministic for a given seed, so the same seed always gives the same map. Herbert Wolverson's recipe for an overworld: tune octaves, gain, lacunarity and frequency (he recommends experimenting in a noise tool), treat the value as altitude, and threshold it into water, land and mountains. Because noise is continuous under zoom, the same tool serves for clouds, particles and wood grain ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 13:59](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=839)).

A single layer looks dull up close. Wolverson's fix is a second, bumpier noise layer whose share of the blend grows as the player zooms in, adding bays, peaks and valleys while the continent stays coherent. Asked how to avoid samey Perlin overworlds, he adds mixing in height values from more mountainous maps for mountain regions, and running an erosion simulation, especially with rocks of varying hardness ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 14:38](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=878)).

### Voronoi and Dijkstra maps

A Voronoi diagram assigns each tile to its nearest seed point. The distance metric sets the feel: Euclidean distance gives smooth edges, Manhattan (taxicab) distance gives sharp, man-made shapes, and Chebyshev sits between. Seeds can be random or placed deliberately; even spacing gives a beehive. Wolverson brute-forces the assignment rather than using Delaunay triangulation ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 10:58](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=658)).

A Dijkstra map floods outward from one or more start points, numbering each walkable tile with its step distance and leaving unreachable tiles at a sentinel value. Wolverson treats it as the basis of many map-checking tasks and recommends RogueBasin's article "The Incredible Power of Dijkstra Maps" ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 19:06](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1146)).

### Cellular automata

Ian Holmes defines cellular automata broadly: any lattice of tiles with local neighbourhood rules, updated synchronously or not. That covers Conway-style counting rules, reaction-diffusion, lookup-table reactions and entity-component cells that respond to messages, possibly updating at different speeds. The core is very localised interaction between a cell and its neighbourhood ([Ian Holmes 2017, 4:03](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=243)).

The neighbourhood is a real choice. Scott Anderson lists von Neumann (the four cardinal neighbours, rarely used for falling sand), Moore (all eight surrounding cells, very common) and Margolus, the one falling-sand games favour. Margolus is a block cellular automaton: it updates each small block in isolation, then offsets the block grid by one on the next update so changes propagate to neighbours, touching a smaller area and fewer cells. He also mentions multi-neighbourhood CA (MNCA) for organic-looking results ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:18:26](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=15506)).

Two speed techniques come from Greg L's bit-twiddling talk:

- **Bit-packed Life.** Store cells as packed bits, compute neighbour sums with a convolution, then apply the birth and survival rules (sum is 2 or 3; cell alive or sum odd) with seven bitwise operations that handle eight cells at once, masking away garbage bits. It runs at 180 frames per second on a Game Boy-class fantasy console ([Greg L 2026, 25:45](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=1545)).
- **Row-at-a-time flood fill.** A per-pixel recursive flood fill over 16,000 tiles is too slow on PICO-8. Treat a row of packed bits as a word, find a run of empty cells with tricks such as subtracting one (which borrows down to the first set bit) and XORing to isolate the changed bits, fill the whole span at once, then recurse to neighbouring rows. Surround the screen with solid so the fill stays bounded ([Greg L 2026, 17:10](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=1030)).

Local rules also build mazes. Josh Galecki's wheat maze in Moondrop grows by repeatedly opening a candidate tile that has exactly one open neighbour and turning candidates with more than one into walls. The result is a loop-free branching maze that usually spans the grid; all its tiles look alike, so players struggle to tell where they are ([Josh Galecki 2023, 10:27](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=627)).

### Case study: Loren Schmidt's inverse terrain solver

Forward methods have known weak spots. Loren Schmidt found noise-based terrain bad at transitions between terrain types, which makes it hard to vary naturally between kinds of geology ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 14:22](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=862)). Physical simulation has the opposite problem: control lives in physical processes and material parameters such as a volcano's magma rate, and if you want islands of a particular width and spacing there is no lever for it ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 13:18](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=798)). bleeptrack hit the same wall outside games: the leaf-vein growth simulation she CNC-milled into a chair's seat and backrest could not be used for the legs, because she could not control how the pattern would come out and the legs had to be sturdy ([bleeptrack 2025, 24:38](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=1478)).

Schmidt's answer is to work backwards. Decide the land/water bitmap first, then compute heights by starting at the shoreline (sea level) and walking uphill inward, adding a height step each time. The heights always agree with the map; a square island becomes a pyramid ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 15:34](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=934)). From there the method is a stack of small, implementable steps:

1. **Noisy steps.** With uniform steps every slope has the same cross-section. Use a random step from a range instead and the slopes turn organic ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 17:40](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1060)).
2. **Lakes.** Find inland lakes by flood-filling and labelling each connected body of water; any body under a size threshold is a lake rather than ocean ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 16:26](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=986)).
3. **Colliding fronts.** Run the uphill solver from sea level and lake shores at the same time. The wave fronts meet and form crescents and peaks, and lakes can never sit above the terrain around them ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 17:06](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1026)).
4. **Continents by voting.** Seed land and ocean and run a voting rule to get cohesive landmasses, then add the features voting would erase, such as inland lakes and island chains. Detect terrain types and populate regions within each to give local geographic flavour ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 27:48](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1668)).
5. **Regional CA rules.** Seed regions by growing random points until they fill space, then run a different eight-neighbour totalistic CA rule in each patch in parallel, drawn from about 201 curated rules, with patch edges interacting as they develop. This governs regional variation such as island clustering and gaps. Schmidt suggests three-state totalistic rules and rules that distinguish diagonal from orthogonal neighbours for finer shaping ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 22:45](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1365)).
6. **Per-terrain fronts.** Give each terrain type its own wave-front speed and noisiness. Clean linear fronts produce fluting for hill-and-gully systems; noisy fronts produce fine hills or small ranges. One mountain type is deliberately overpiled above its angle of repose and then settled to the angle its terrain type specifies ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 29:11](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1751)).

Because the solver separates the land/water map from height generation, the map can come from anywhere: conventional techniques, hand-made patches, or a mix. Schmidt suggests hand-making large features, such as a village on a peninsula, so players learn them, while procedural detail surprises them on each playthrough ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 21:24](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1284)).

> You can make the whole map or patches of it by hand and then shake out details procedurally. — [Loren Schmidt 2024, 21:24](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1284)

### Geometry: procedural meshes

Adrian Herbez's 3D-printable generators show the geometric end of the toolkit. In three.js you build a mesh by pushing vertex positions into a list, then defining triangle faces as triples of vertex indices; faces hold no positional data. For a cube, number the eight vertices in a sensible order (around the bottom, then the top) and add two triangles per square face ([Adrian Herbez 2020, 5:50](https://youtu.be/SMQuoI_M-kk?t=350)). The first step toward a procedural shape is replacing hard-coded coordinates with parameters, such as width, height and depth read from HTML inputs, halved and substituted for the unit coordinates ([Adrian Herbez 2020, 8:49](https://youtu.be/SMQuoI_M-kk?t=529)). For printing, wind every face counter-clockwise as seen from outside: faces exist from one side only, defined by the normal, and slicing software relies on outward-facing normals ([Adrian Herbez 2020, 6:31](https://youtu.be/SMQuoI_M-kk?t=391)).

## Generating from examples: wave function collapse and its relatives

### One routine, many maps

Brian Bucklew says that for twenty years he would have written a bespoke algorithm for each kind of map. In Caves of Qud, walled compounds, aqueducts, salt towers and villages, maps of very different character, come from one wave function collapse (WFC) routine fed different tiny training images. WFC was released by Maxim Gumin in 2016, and Qud was its first commercial use ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 2:06](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=126)). The appeal is the workflow: a designer draws a tiny input in a paint program and gets arbitrarily large outputs that are locally similar to it. Rooms-and-halls, squiggly caverns and a line-and-dots pattern that would traditionally need a recursive builder, cellular automata and a custom line drawer all come from the same code ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 4:33](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=273)). A five-minute MS Paint sketch of a temple or garden gave Bucklew layouts he says would take a week to approximate with BSP trees and noise maps ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 13:09](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=789)).

> All of these maps are produced by the exact same technique, literally the same block of code with some tiny different little training inputs. — [Brian Bucklew 2019, 2:06](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=126)

### How it works

Bucklew's intuition is a pile of cards. Cut the input into every overlapping N×N patch (3×3 in Qud), multiplied by rotations and reflections: a 10×10 image yields 100 cards, up to 800 with symmetry. Put the full set of cards on every output pixel. Then repeatedly find the shortest stack left, pick a random card from it, and remove incompatible overlapping cards from nearby stacks, recursing until the image resolves. He likens it to Markov chaining words, in two dimensions ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 6:41](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=401)).

Adam Newgas gives the solver's view. Every tile starts possible in every output cell; the algorithm picks a cell, assigns one of its still-possible tiles, and propagates the rules learned from the sample to rule out tiles in neighbouring cells, using the AC3 arc-consistency algorithm from constraint solvers. Because each pick is made only among tiles already consistent with the rules, the output grows into an image locally similar to the sample but larger, with potentially different global structure ([Adam Newgas 2022, 5:54](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=354)). In the common **overlapped** variant, every 3×3 patch of the output must match some 3×3 patch of the input, possibly rotated or reflected ([Adam Newgas 2022, 6:47](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=407)). Its ancestor, **model synthesis**, learns only which tiles may be adjacent, so a bridge learned next to river tiles stays next to rivers, but a forest that was not adjacent to the bridge is free to move, producing global structure the sample did not contain ([Adam Newgas 2022, 7:40](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=460)). Sergio Garces offers a lighter explanation: it is like playing Carcassonne where you may place any tile as long as edges match. He used it in Mekanical Armada to lay out roads, which could not just be random tiles and still make sense ([Sergio Garces 2022, 20:12](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1212)).

Getting started is cheap. The reference implementation takes about three lines of code and a few parameters: input image, output size, whether to tile at the edges, and a symmetry value from 0 to 8. Bucklew advises setting symmetry to the maximum at first for non-oriented results, then lowering it when you want specific orientations ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 15:00](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=900)).

### Controls

Newgas notes that Caves of Qud, Bad North, Townscaper and Infinite WaveFunctionCollapse all use WFC, and none uses it exactly as first described; part of the algorithm's appeal is how easily it can be varied ([Adam Newgas 2022, 3:25](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=205)). The talks describe these levers:

- **Encode meaning as colour.** A plain black square as input gave shapes with no clear inside or outside. When Bucklew marked the inside of the square in red, every turn kept red on the same side and the output became enclosed buildings, which he calls "extremely controllable" ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 12:10](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=730)).
- **Hero pieces.** Split a large hand-made piece into multi-cell tiles with rules that allow only one possible neighbour for each part. Once one tile is placed, the whole piece is inserted verbatim but still joins the surrounding generation ([Adam Newgas 2022, 9:37](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=577)).
- **Painted edges instead of a sample.** Annotate tiles with edge types (green connects to green, brown to brown). Covering every combination with a sample makes the sample grow exponentially; edge rules scale better to big tile sets ([Adam Newgas 2022, 10:09](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=609)).
- **Inpainting.** Fix some tiles in advance, by hand, by another algorithm or by the player, and let WFC fill around them, guaranteeing the generated tiles connect consistently ([Adam Newgas 2022, 11:13](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=673)). Bucklew notes advanced variants can fill in around hand-placed seeds such as cities dropped into an overworld ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 24:09](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=1449)).
- **Region-driven weights.** The choice of which cell and which tile to pick can be any heuristic and the result stays valid. Qud uses its own region decisions to tell WFC which tiles and weights to use in each area, so one algorithm makes ruins here and forest there; Newgas also shows a temple complex filtered by an overall yin-yang image ([Adam Newgas 2022, 12:30](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=750)).
- **No randomness at all.** Townscaper always picks the highest-priority tile that fits, and the player paints what they want while WFC chooses tiles and keeps them consistent ([Adam Newgas 2022, 11:13](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=673)). The solver's inference then produces consequences the designer did not plan: add a house that closes off an area and grass, a high-priority tile, becomes possible where a low-priority patch had to go before ([Adam Newgas 2022, 13:48](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=828)).

### Limits

The talks that use WFC converge on its weaknesses, and the main ones trace back to the fact that it only knows local similarity.

- **Homogeneous output.** It repeats on the scale of its input, and a huge locally similar map is not necessarily one you want to play ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 15:30](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=930)). Qud's developers say WFC interiors look the same in every direction ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 47:40](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2860)).
- **Overfitting.** With a very detailed input of many colours there is only one way tiles can overlap, so the input is just repeated. Bucklew's attempts to encode doors and furniture in the input narrowed the output's variety ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 16:21](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=981)); a star-shaped input gave less variety for the same reason ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 13:09](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=789)).
- **Cost.** It is quick on small inputs and very slow on large inputs and outputs ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 15:30](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=930)). Large ordered structures, such as Greco-Roman temples with big columns, need a large window, which drives memory too high for mobile, so Qud uses WFC mostly where the window can be small, such as ruins and small villages ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 22:17](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=1337)).
- **Contradictions.** WFC is not a complete solver and occasionally contradicts itself; Qud simply retries, since in practice failures are rare and maps usually generate in a fraction of a millisecond ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 24:09](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=1449)).
- **Order of generation.** It grows outward from an initial state, so it does not suit worlds generated cell by cell in arbitrary order ([Alexander Birke 2024, 5:36](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=336)).

Qud's fix for homogeneity is structural: generate one of several kinds of higher-level structure, such as a circular tower, and fill its interior with WFC ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 47:40](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2860)). Let WFC supply texture inside a frame something else decides.

### Global constraints and Halina's TRP

Emily Halina presses the local-only limit further. In a key-and-door dungeon (GVG-AI's Zelda, where the player must get a key and then reach a door), WFC produced levels with keys but no door and spiders sealed in their own chambers; it only respects constraints visible locally in the example, and Markov chains share the problem ([Emily Halina 2024, 22:26](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1346)). The usual alternative, constructive generation, where designers author "Lego pieces" that an authored generator assembles as in Enter the Gungeon, Hades, Isaac and Slay the Spire, is expressive but expensive: someone must author every piece, the generator, and often constraint metadata such as a room that only fits in a corner ([Emily Halina 2024, 2:45](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=165)).

Halina's tree-based reconstructive partitioning (TRP) learns from a single example without asking the designer to write constraints. A Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) agent plays a human-made source level; the search tree becomes the skeleton of a new level; details are filled in by copying matched segments of the original; threats are placed probabilistically. The designer only tweaks a few parameters ([Emily Halina 2024, 5:45](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=345)). In steps:

1. **Binary reconstruction.** Every tile the simulated player visited becomes empty and everything else solid, giving a cavernous outline of a traversable path. MCTS also records where the player died or the level became uncompletable; the designer specifies which tiles count as empty and full ([Emily Halina 2024, 11:15](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=675)). More playthroughs give a less restricted level, because the stochastic search takes different routes each time, which suits games with branching paths ([Emily Halina 2024, 14:33](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=873)).
2. **Partitioning.** Split the sketch into randomly sized segments, and for each one scan the original level for the section whose solid/empty layout is closest by edit distance, choosing randomly among ties, and paste it in. A path where Mario jumped from one pipe to another gets matched with a two-pipe structure ([Emily Halina 2024, 12:16](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=736)).

Segment size is the main dial, trading plagiarism against chaos. Larger segments copy more of the original, which is not always bad: a Mario level without its final staircase would feel wrong. Small segments give chaotic but sometimes useful output, such as floating structures for games with more vertical movement ([Emily Halina 2024, 15:09](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=909)). On Zelda, the TRP level resembled the original with moved walls and enemies but stayed completable, while WFC and Markov outputs were mostly unplayable. Deriving the skeleton from a successful playthrough is what carries the global "get the key, then the door" constraint ([Emily Halina 2024, 23:18](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1398)). TRP can also use human playthroughs or A* instead of MCTS, though one human path captures fewer alternative routes than a search tree, and it can blend several source levels, such as Mario 1-1 and 1-2 ([Emily Halina 2024, 32:36](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1956)). Halina expects it to struggle on logic-heavy puzzles like Sokoban, because partitioning only reasons about local sections and ignores global solvability ([Emily Halina 2024, 24:33](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1473)).

### When to reach for example-based generation

Example-based methods pay off when the character you want is easier to draw than to describe: a designer can paint a small sample in minutes and get texture that would take a week of bespoke code ([Brian Bucklew 2019, 4:33](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=273); [Brian Bucklew 2019, 13:09](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=789)). They are weak where the level must satisfy global properties, such as progression, solvability or large-scale order, that no local window can see ([Emily Halina 2024, 22:26](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1346); [Brian Bucklew 2019, 22:17](https://youtu.be/fnFj3dOKcIQ?t=1337)). For those, either wrap the example-based generator inside constructive structure, as Qud does ([Jason Grinblat et al. 2018, 47:40](https://youtu.be/owmGknfj6H4?t=2860)), or take the global skeleton from something that understands play, as TRP does ([Emily Halina 2024, 23:18](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1398)), and accept that fully constructive generation buys control at the price of authoring every piece ([Emily Halina 2024, 2:45](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=165)).

## Describe the result, not the steps: constraint solving and search

Most generators are recipes: carve a room, then a corridor, then place a door. Constraint-based generation inverts that. You state what a finished output must be like, and a solver searches for one. Adam Newgas frames the move as taking an ordinary solving technique and injecting randomness so that it becomes a generator; the appeal is that you never have to write construction rules directly, yet the output is still varied ([Adam Newgas 2022, 2:10](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=130)). Wave function collapse, covered earlier in this chapter, is one instance of this family, and Newgas presents it that way ([Adam Newgas 2022, 2:10](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=130)).

Two benefits come with the inversion. Pierre Vigier argues constraints are intuitive to write (if you want the shower in the corner, you add a constraint saying so) and that they give strong guarantees: any solution the solver returns satisfies every constraint by definition ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 3:03](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=183)). Isaac Karth makes a related point about Spelunky, which he calls *cohesive*: because its generator can only place elements that fit together, you can throw any settings at it and still get a usable level. He adds the limit: cohesion does not help if the generator is assembling the wrong things ([Isaac Karth 2019, 19:16](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=1156)).

### Don't write your own solver by accident

Kate Compton's 2016 warning is about what happens without a solver. Hand-written generators tend either to generate and throw away much of their output or to get neutered into trivial results, such as a straight line because that is the only layout that reliably reaches the exit. Some teams discovered they were really writing a constraint solver and spent years on it, when mature solvers representing around a hundred PhD-years of tuning already existed ([Kate Compton 2016, 21:46](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1306)). Her recommendation is off-the-shelf tools such as answer set programming (ASP, a logic-programming approach where you declare facts and rules and a solver finds models that satisfy them). She points to Adam Smith's map-generation speedrun with ASP, which builds a heavily constrained ASCII map generator that requires the player to pass the key before reaching the exit, the kind of rule that is hard to hand-code. Her group uses the Clingo solver, which she concedes is hard to learn ([Kate Compton 2016, 21:24](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1284)).

> They're hard to learn, but writing your own can be worse. — [Kate Compton 2016, 21:46](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1306)

### Implementing a constraint satisfaction problem

Vigier's room-furnishing talk is specific enough to build from. Frame the room as a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP): one variable per object to place, each with a domain of all its possible positions, plus constraints such as "the room stays connected" or "this object goes against a wall" or "in a corner". A solution is an assignment of a position to every variable such that all constraints hold. He applies the same frame to monsters, furniture and decorations in dungeons or buildings, and to outdoor structures like swamps or marketplaces ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 2:08](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=128)).

The solver is backtracking search, under ten lines: assign variables one at a time, check constraints after each assignment, and back up when a variable's domain runs out. It finds a solution if one exists. On its own it is deterministic, because it tries values in the same order every time; to turn it into a generator, shuffle each domain before you start. Variable order need not be random, and taking the variable with the smallest remaining domain first (the minimum-remaining-values heuristic) speeds it up significantly ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 4:29](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=269)).

Speed then comes from making each constraint check cheap ([Pierre Vigier 2022, 10:16](https://youtu.be/oVhq8V93gHM?t=616)):

- **Unary constraints** (about one object alone) are applied once, up front, by pruning the domain: "against a wall" keeps only the positions in the first row; "in a corner" keeps the four corners.
- **No overlap** is tracked with an occupancy grid updated incrementally as objects are placed and removed.
- **Connectivity** needs a depth-first search over free tiles, which is expensive to run after every assignment. Skip it whenever the free tiles are certainly still one connected piece; Vigier reports roughly an order-of-magnitude speedup from that check alone.

The same pattern extends to propagation-based solvers. Newgas shows that any rule able to say "placing this tile here would cause a problem", such as keeping a path connected end to end, can be bolted onto wave function collapse by running it at every step of the propagation loop. Several such rules run in sequence, each with a veto, to enforce properties the example image never taught the algorithm ([Adam Newgas 2022, 14:53](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=893)).

### Search by brute force, and how to make it tractable

Not every search needs a formal solver. Jack Schlesinger describes Knotwords' first generator, loosely inspired by binary space partitioning dungeons: fill the grid randomly with fitting words until space runs out, then step backward through earlier decisions trying alternatives, for example swapping "yak" for another word to close remaining gaps. He is clear that this only fills the space; it does nothing to make the puzzle good or appropriately difficult ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 12:27](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=747)).

Dead Cells shows how far plain brute force can go in a shipped game. Sébastien "deepnight" Benard explains that the game turns its abstract node tree into a level by randomly picking rooms of the needed type, fitting them by matching exits, and backtracking on overlap. A single level often takes 5,000 to 10,000 tries, more for complex layouts. The prototype's fitter was never replaced; it is what the loading screens are doing. Evil Empire later sped it up by discarding obviously failing cases early, but it is still brute force and players don't care ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 23:56](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1436)).

When the space is too big even for that, the ordering of choices matters. droqen's Sudoku-poem tool places words so that the givens of a Sudoku spell a phrase. Trying every permutation of word positions and running a Sudoku solver on each was far too slow. Noticing that "kill" only works where its double L straddles a row seam, he generalised the observation into a function that picks the word with the fewest immediately viable placements, places it first, and branches over the remaining words from there. Cheap tests, such as a repeated letter in one row, reject a placement before the full solver ever runs ([droqen 2026, 14:01](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=841)). Starting from a long word helps for the same reason: it cuts the search space hardest ([droqen 2026, 19:30](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1170)). This is the same instinct as Vigier's smallest-domain-first heuristic: commit early to the most constrained choice, and fail fast.

### What constraints cost

The first cost is contradiction. Newgas warns that the more rules you add to a wave function collapse generator, the more likely it hits contradictions that make it run forever or return nothing, and he calls contradictions one of the key hang-ups of this kind of generation ([Adam Newgas 2022, 15:15](https://youtu.be/CS5MUwiVTYE?t=915)).

The second is that content constraints take away the designer's usual fixes. droqen's project replaces Sudoku digits with a nine-letter alphabet; the phrase must use every letter so the alphabet is fully defined, or the puzzle will have multiple solutions ([droqen 2026, 22:42](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1362)). A real Sudoku needs exactly one solution. When an ordinary puzzle designer sees an ambiguity between two fives, they add another five as a clue; droqen could not, because there is no extra five in pi, so most of his hand-encoded messages yielded unsolvable or non-unique puzzles ([droqen 2026, 8:28](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=508)). Once he had built the search tool, he found that phrases yielding a valid Sudoku are rare: his Magpie poem produced ten valid variants, but most phrases he tried produced nothing at all ([droqen 2026, 20:47](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1247)). Stack enough constraints and valid outputs become needles. Even then, droqen found the constraints did not settle everything: where the digits went, whether to stack them vertically or let them run diagonally, remained aesthetic decisions, and different encodings of the same message gave visibly different shapes ([droqen 2026, 6:03](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=363)).

The third cost is that some properties resist local rules. Ian Holmes, asked about architectural-looking levels, calls symmetry a global property that rule systems working locally struggle to produce. He suggests combining grammars with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods that stochastically optimise a global cost function, citing procedural alibi generation, which searches NPC backstories until they fit everything the player has seen ([Ian Holmes 2017, 17:52](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=1072)).

### Beyond space: optimisation at runtime

Constraint solving and search are not only for maps. Mark Gritter's Emoji Economy has to allocate each good among competing uses (eat the apples, make juice, make apple butter), and the shares must sum to 100%. Because the utility objective is nonlinear, linear programming is ruled out, so the game uses gradient descent: move in the direction that improves utility, take smaller steps after a step that made things worse, and project any choice that exceeds 100% back to the nearest valid point using a simple published projection algorithm ([Mark Gritter 2020, 5:56](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=356)). If your generator produces systems rather than places, the "describe the result" approach still applies; the solver just changes.

## Guaranteeing the output works: solvability, validation and failure

Constraint solvers guarantee what they are told to; most generators guarantee nothing until you check. Chapter 9 covers guaranteeing a playable level in level-generation terms; this section is about the general strategies. A generator that is right most of the time is not finished. Benard sets the bar for a shipped game: you can write a dungeon generator in five minutes, but one that produces good, interesting results every time takes months, and one that is half trash is not acceptable. The work also forced his team to define what a good result was, which they did not know when they began ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 15:04](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=904)).

Herbert Wolverson states the principle several talks share as the point of his whole talk: guide your randomness, then use algorithms to check that the result matches what you want. His example is a lock-and-key generator that, left unchecked, could put the key behind its own door ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:35](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1475)). Jack Schlesinger explains why checking cannot be left to intuition. Computers do exactly what they are told, even when it is a mistake, and they are bad at judging whether a step is easy or hard for a human; there are too many generated puzzles to review by hand, so the generator needs ways of culling and scoring its output ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 7:59](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=479)). Yet the same machine is what makes generation worthwhile for puzzles: computers are far better than people at checking solvability and uniqueness, a human usually has to solve a puzzle to know it has a solution, and a hand-authored game caps its puzzles at the level of a designer whom good players should eventually outgrow ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 4:23](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=263)).

### Which failures you can afford

Not every flaw needs a guarantee. Brian Walker draws the line in Brogue terms: a generator can tolerate an occasional edge-case failure, such as an inaccessible reward room, but never one that blocks progress, such as an unreachable down staircase. Always check that the downstairs are reachable from the upstairs, and never let passability depend on destructible terrain. In his platformer, explosives arrive late, alongside mobility items, teleporters and extra lives that act as safety valves, and players who deliberately break a level accept the result. His own test of ambition: if it works in 100% of cases, you aren't being ambitious enough ([Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804)).

Use this as your triage. Spend your guarantees on the critical path, and let decorative or optional content fail now and then.

### Strategies for guaranteeing solvability

**Generate and test.** The simplest strategy is to generate, check, and discard failures. Stella Mazeika says this is how most randomizers ensure shuffled key items stay beatable: place the items, check that each is reachable, and if not, throw the whole placement away and try again. Naive shuffling otherwise creates deadlocks such as needing the flippers to reach the gloves and the gloves to reach the flippers. The cost is generation time, which grows with the number of dependencies and locations; a few newer randomizers use logic or constraint systems instead, and Mazeika wrote the one constraint-based randomizer she knows of ([Stella Mazeika 2019, 6:53](https://youtu.be/C7laugXEc9s?t=413)). Ben Berman puts the strategy in formal terms: every heuristic roguelike level generator is a special case of Markov chain Monte Carlo design, which keeps generating until output fits designer-specified measures such as symmetry or good room layout. The difference is that in a heuristic generator the designer chooses the criteria by hand rather than the computer working them out ([Ben Berman 2017, 8:27](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=507)). The same family of methods can guide detail as well as accept or reject it; Berman shows Daniel Ritchie's work refining a blocked-out spaceship into a detailed one and arranging furniture in a room over time, which he suggests could help 3D roguelikes without tiles, where decorating rooms is hard ([Ben Berman 2017, 12:03](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=723)).

**Analytic: prove every output is solvable.** Josh Galecki, drawing on his maths and computer science training, distinguishes two ways to guarantee solvable puzzles. The *analytic* way proves that every configuration in the space can be solved; the *constructive* way builds each puzzle around a known solution ([Josh Galecki 2023, 3:14](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=194)). Moondrop's 2x4 Lights Out lantern puzzle is his analytic example. Toggling a switch twice cancels out regardless of moves in between; sequences exist that toggle the top-left and top-middle switches alone; board symmetry extends those to all eight. Together these prove every state is solvable, so the game can start from any random configuration, the designer never needs to know the solution, and a minimal solution takes at most eight moves ([Josh Galecki 2023, 6:12](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=372)). When you can find such a proof, generation is free: any random state will do.

**Constructive: build the solution in.** Galecki's river-grid puzzle in Moondrop is a 4x4 directed graph where water flows down and right and each vertex's level is the sum of its incoming edges. He places locked dams, then the toggleable dams that must be closed and must be open, records the target water levels at four vertices, and only then randomises the toggles before the player arrives. A solution exists because that is how he built it; extra solutions are fine ([Josh Galecki 2023, 9:32](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=572)). His advice is that it is easiest to start from a solution and add red herrings and traps, and possible but riskier to build up toward one ([Josh Galecki 2023, 12:23](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=743)). Good Sudoku follows the same pattern: Schlesinger's team starts from a filled valid grid, which is easy to make, and removes digits in pairs mirrored across the centre, re-running a solver after each removal to confirm the puzzle is still valid ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 11:43](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=703)).

**Build a solver, and reuse it.** That validating solver earns its cost twice. Schlesinger's team drew on the Sudoku community's catalogued techniques and "deadly patterns", which made ambiguity easy to detect; when the solver hit an ambiguity, the generator knew to go back. As a side effect, the solver powers a verbose hint system ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 15:53](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=953)).

**Refine instead of restarting.** You need not throw away a whole output to fix part of it. Schlesinger compares Knotwords to cellular-automaton cave smoothing, which removes isolated wall pillars while keeping clustered walls.
