In Knotwords the team keeps regions it likes, such as a good top-left corner, removes the region it doesn't, and steps through better English words to refill it, ending with a cleaner puzzle with less common words and more vowel variety ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 24:46](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1486)).

### How guarantees fail

Search-based generators can fail silently. Galecki's Moondrop maze could, if the algorithm picked the wrong one of two final candidate tiles, wall off its last tile and become unsolvable. His fix: when no open neighbour is found, carve a path toward the start until one is. That guarantees solvability but gives up the maze's no-loops property. The general lesson he draws is that if your algorithm searches for the solution, you must hunt for the counterexample ([Josh Galecki 2023, 11:13](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=673)).

> If your algorithm is searching for the solution you have to be aware of the bugs, and in math speak you have to look for the counter example. — [Josh Galecki 2023, 11:13](https://youtu.be/6vMxH6OtI54?t=673)

Patching a failure in place can be worse than regenerating. Aaron A. Reed traces this through Star Trek (1971). Mayfield's original, at line 775, simply restarted generation if the galaxy had no starbase or no Klingon. A later cleanup replaced the restart with a single line that forced one quadrant to a fixed code. That clever-looking fix introduced three bugs: it no longer handled zero Klingons, it changed the counts after they had been shown to the player, and it failed to update the global counters the game used to track the win state, so the game could fail to end ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 15:50](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=950)). Regenerating is crude, but it keeps every invariant the generator already maintains; overwriting part of an output means re-establishing all of them yourself.

### Counterweight: not every output needs checking

All this can push you toward constraining everything. Two talks push back. Alexei Pepers reports that the Caves of Qud team keeps generators unconstrained by default and adds only minimal constraints once a specific negative impact is proven. She found this surprising, since constraining generators is common advice. For creature placement, a difficulty constraint stops lethal late-game creatures appearing in starting areas, and a biome constraint keeps a sense of place, such as fungi in fungal forests ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 40:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2437)). Bjarke Alexander Larsen, building a repeatable logic puzzle in a Discord bot, concludes that you can sometimes get away with unchecked randomness if players have a good way of dealing with the bad outcomes ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 16:20](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=980)).

These positions are not in conflict with Wolverson's or Walker's so much as they locate the line differently. The deciding question is who pays when an output is bad. If a bad output blocks progress, check it ([Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804)). If the player has a way to deal with it ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 16:20](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=980)), Qud's practice suggests leaving the generator free until you can name the harm ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 40:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2437)).

## Grammars and corpora: generating text and structure from rules

The techniques for generating text divide roughly into grammars, which expand symbols into text according to rules you write, and corpus methods, which recombine text you collect. In practice the strongest systems mix them.

### Grammars: assembling human-written chunks

Kate Compton's Tracery is the reference point for many speakers. It is a reusable templating grammar: you write a small JSON file of symbols and rules, and it recursively expands phrases whose symbols refer to other phrases. Compton built it so that nobody would have to build their own templating text system again, comparing it to the one Kingdom of Loathing built. It has been ported to Python, Ruby, Unity, Twine and more, and through the Cheap Bots Done Quick host it runs hundreds of Twitter bots ([Kate Compton 2016, 2:49](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=169)). Martin Pichlmair used it for a recipe bot and notes that games such as Caves of Qud use it too; producing grammatical sentences is a known difficulty, which he says Qud somehow handles ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 12:09](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=729)). At the far end of the novelty spectrum, a 2017 lightning talk described a joke compiler from Tracery grammars to Ethereum smart contracts, which its maker billed as the world's most expensive way to generate a bit of text ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 8:36](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=516)).

Bruno Dias's Voyageur shows how to make grammar text read well. Its descriptions are built mostly from large, human-written chunks, usually whole sentences, through a Tracery-like recursive grammar that picks a paragraph structure, then sentences, then words; little of the text varies down to the individual word ([Bruno Dias 2016, 6:32](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=392)). The key move is filtering. Following Emily Short's Annals of the Parrigues, where the generator commits to statements as it goes and builds an increasingly detailed internal model, Voyageur first picks baseline facts about a planet (some inherited from region templates, some random), then chooses phrases by priority rules that favour aspects not yet mentioned or a randomly chosen focal aspect ([Bruno Dias 2016, 7:33](https://youtu.be/UGPkEWqwSAY?t=453)). The grammar supplies variety; the model keeps the description consistent and moving forward.

Kingdom of Loathing reached similar machinery on its own, and Zack Johnson's account is a practical checklist:

- **Word buckets.** Text fields in the database from which a function pulls a random line, optionally filtered, for example by starting letter or index. Even structured content such as hobo names (first name, last name) adds only a little structure on top ([Zack Johnson 2016, 8:06](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=486)).
- **Grammar handling.** The team wanted generated writing to be grammatically correct, so its "mad lib" template function handles automatic *a*/*an*, proper-noun capitalisation (to build place names such as a random "colorville"), singular and plural, and gendered forms ([Zack Johnson 2016, 12:28](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=748)).
- **State within a generation.** A "unique" option asks a bucket for distinct values, so a lizard is never blue with blue stripes; a "reuse" option repeats an earlier pick so the same random thing can be referred to again ([Zack Johnson 2016, 14:06](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=846)).
- **Rare absurdity by design.** The adjective bucket can call itself, so lucky rolls produce "big big big big big ugly Dan". Johnson's point is to build such recursion in so that it happens only once in a while, which is what makes it remarkable and funny ([Zack Johnson 2016, 14:42](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=882)).

### Grammars formally, and why they are hard to author

Abdelrahman Madkour gives the formal definition. A generative grammar is a string-rewriting system: start from a sentence, find a non-terminal symbol, and replace it using a rule whose left-hand side matches, until only terminals remain. Each rule's left side is a non-terminal; its right side mixes terminals and non-terminals. Grammars came from linguistics and now underlie city and building generation ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 13:22](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=802)). His warning is that they are hard to author because rules do not map intuitively to outputs. That is why grammar tools such as CityEngine (a shape grammar for buildings) and SpeedTree (L-systems for trees) are specialised to one domain, and why you cannot reuse them to generate, say, guns ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 15:48](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=948)). Expect to iterate by running the grammar and looking, not by reasoning from the rules.

### Graph grammars: rewriting structure, keeping invariants

The same idea works on graphs. A graph grammar finds a subgraph matching a rule's left-hand side and replaces it with the right-hand side; nodes might be rooms and edges doors or paths. Madkour presents it as the representation behind Joris Dormans-style mission generation ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 19:35](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1175)). Mark Gritter uses graph grammars for economies in Emoji Economy, where production rules match labelled nodes and edges and alter them: one rule inserts a new plant between a source and the sink; a more complex one adds an alternative process producing the same good plus an unconnected byproduct that later rules can use or turn into negative-utility garbage ([Mark Gritter 2020, 3:08](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=188)).

Gritter names the strength: graph grammars make it easy to preserve structural invariants. Dormans' Unexplored never puts a key behind the door it opens, and Emoji Economy keeps every good's inputs and outputs hooked up so no consumable is left unused ([Mark Gritter 2020, 3:37](https://youtu.be/Q_MFTUYnaf0?t=217)). If your rules each preserve the invariant, every output does, with no separate validation pass. That is a guarantee of the constructive kind described in the previous section.

### Corpora: the source is the design

Markov chains are the classic corpus method. Jason Grinblat's construction: map each n-word prefix in the corpus to the list of words that follow it, then generate by repeatedly choosing a random follower for the current prefix. In "the cat isn't sleeping but the cat is definitely not listening", the order-2 prefix "the cat" maps to both "isn't" and "is". Punctuation is kept. The order *n* controls predictability: a high enough order just reproduces the corpus, and Caves of Qud uses order two ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 5:38](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=338)). Everest Pipkin gives the same mechanism from "it was the best of times", where "it was" can be followed by "the best", "the age" or "the epoch", and explains why the output feels semi-grammatical yet falls apart in obvious ways ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 7:50](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=470)).

Grinblat's central claim is that what makes Markov text interesting is the clever choice and arrangement of the corpus, not the generation rules, which are simple. His examples mixed Puppet documentation with H. P. Lovecraft, and LinkedIn recruiter emails with drug-use anecdotes ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 8:07](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=487)). Pipkin, who curates poetic corpora, converges from the other side: large corpora produce interesting work when artists hand-define rules and constraints that sit on top of the corpus rather than relying on its raw content. Her examples include Allison Parrish's work with a three-million-line Gutenberg poetry corpus, a bot that collects tweets in iambic pentameter into an endless sonnet, and Jonathan Basile's Library of Babel ([Everest Pipkin 2019, 16:08](https://youtu.be/IYNKs8vfocc?t=968)). Read together: the corpus is your raw material and your style, and the rules are your editorial hand.

> The clever arrangement of the corpus, the clever choice of a corpus, rather than the rules of actually generating the text. — [Jason Grinblat 2016, 8:07](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=487)

Grinblat also shows how to tune a Markov generator precisely. A prefix appears in generated text at roughly the frequency it appears in the corpus, which he found by frequency analysis of Qud's chain. That makes common prefixes such as "in the" and "to the" usable as hooks for inserting hand-written content ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 19:10](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1150)). Caves of Qud embeds secrets in its generated books this way, and the rate is set by a formula: secrets to add equals desired secrets per book, times the average number of suffixes per hook, divided by hooks per book. "In the" has around a hundred suffixes. Grinblat aimed for about one secret every four books ([Jason Grinblat 2016, 22:07](https://youtu.be/zDTQM0Ipiz4?t=1327)).

### Names from sound systems

Sraëka-Lillian builds name generators from phonology, the study of a language's sound system and the patterns that shape it. The procedure has three components: a phonemic inventory (which sounds the language has), rules for combining sounds into syllables, and techniques for smoothing where syllables, roots and suffixes join ([Sraëka-Lillian 2021, 6:11](https://youtu.be/XQKNwaCwD-I?t=371)). Because names come from a consistent sound system, a culture's names sound related to each other rather than randomly assembled.

### Form as a generated constraint

Clarissa Littler's poetry project generates form rather than words, for a human poet to fill. Because poetry spans many forms, she built a family of generators rather than one, starting from the simplest: stanzas of lines whose lengths vary randomly around a mean, shown as dashes per syllable. That produced something like modern free verse, but only a sliver of what poetry can be ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 2:07](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=127)). Her later generators are worth borrowing for any rhythmic or layout content:

- **Summed waves.** Line length as a function of line and stanza number, built by adding randomly chosen pre-made wave pieces. The result is smooth and varied without feeling either too regular or janky ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 4:42](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=282)).
- **Signal functions.** A wave varying across a line: wherever its value is at or above zero, place a syllable; below zero, a space. This interleaves text and white space into broken, deconstructed lines, which generating indentation separately had failed to do ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 6:23](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=383)).
- **Grab-bag rhymes.** Pick a number of rhyme endings proportional to poem length, at most about half the line count, and assign them randomly to lines. It produces natural-looking schemes and occasional oddities, such as every line on one sound, which she embraced and softened with slant rhymes ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 9:02](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=542)).

Her warning applies to constraint-based generation generally. There is a sweet spot between freedom and constraint; combining generated stress patterns with rhyme felt over-constrained, more like solving a puzzle than writing poetry ([Clarissa Littler 2020, 10:35](https://youtu.be/OzCGTXakbjE?t=635)). droqen met the same wall from the other side in his Sudoku poems, described under constraint solving above.

## Generating rules, histories and stories

Levels and text are the comfortable targets. This section covers generators that make the stranger things: the rules of the game itself, the past of its world, and the stories that unfold in it.

### Generating mechanics

Mike Cook argues that roguelikes tend to use procedural generation only for things designers are comfortable generating. Even Brogue's generated levels are full of familiar things like doors, and he wants players to meet genuinely new ways to interact with the world: a match-three where swiping subtracts numbers, or Breakout where each brick hit triggers a new rule. He means hand-built generators, not large language models ([Mike Cook 2023, 3:19](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=199)). He then lays out a ladder of approaches, from safest to most expressive.

1. **Rearrange modular content.** Toggle and combine options that already exist to vary a run or campaign, as Invisible, Inc. does with campaign settings and Slay the Spire does with daily-challenge modifiers. Modifiers compound: allowing green cards plus starting with five copies of a random card can give five green cards ([Mike Cook 2023, 11:16](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=676)).
2. **Design languages.** Noita's wand programming, Baba Is You's rule sentences and Caves of Qud's mod data are constrained but expressive languages for describing mechanics, and a generator can write in them too. Designers already build such languages for modders; scoping one to a domain such as spells or potions trades expressivity for focus. Cook used this approach in ANGELINA and Puck ([Mike Cook 2023, 13:11](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=791)). The catch is that a generator has no common sense. Modders learn a tool's limits through play; a generator doesn't, so the language itself must make illegal or absurd statements, such as negative hit points, hard to write, or they will cause glitches and crashes. Cook also notes the "PuzzleScript effect": tools are remembered for their most limit-pushing uses, while AI tends to use the central, intended features ([Mike Cook 2023, 16:28](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=988)).
3. **Generate code directly.** Code is just text, and we know how to generate text. Unity's C# can compile text into an assembly at runtime, which is more expressive than any domain-specific language and stays linked to the codebase as it changes. Cook's tool Pixy is shown the parts of the codebase it may use, with attributes marking data it may or may not touch, and fills an empty code block; it produced a Breakout mechanic where the ball grows. Cook stresses that it knows only your codebase ([Mike Cook 2023, 17:40](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1060)). His advice on constraining it: restrict numbers to sensible ranges, but otherwise give it freedom, because most of the interesting results came from things he forgot to forbid ([Mike Cook 2023, 28:54](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1734)).

How do you filter generated mechanics when you cannot write down what "good" means? Cook's answer is to construct a test scenario. In Pixy, put the player in an unwinnable situation where they die next turn, generate an item, have them use it on themselves, and repeat hundreds of times. Any item that saves them is interesting, whatever it does. This works whenever you can recognise a good result even if you cannot specify one ([Mike Cook 2023, 24:00](https://youtu.be/3daNITP9vBc?t=1440)).

### Generating histories

A world's past can be generated without simulating it. Jason Grinblat explains that Caves of Qud's sultan histories pick each event at random, then rationalise a cause by querying the sultan's earlier events. A sultan saved by dogs later randomly besieged a city; the description generator found her relationship with dogs and wrote that she fought to liberate them. In Q&A he adds that a Tracery-like grammar is driven by internal state, so being liked by a faction enables a rule such as "liberate faction" ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 19:14](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1154)). The causality is apparent rather than real, and it costs a fraction of a simulation.

> There's no actual inherent cause and effect to the system; we're just picking events randomly. — [Jason Grinblat 2017, 19:14](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1154)

Bjarke Alexander Larsen goes the other way for his corrupted-database puzzle, because the puzzle needs a ground truth. He simulates 50 to 100 years of people moving house: each person gets an initial address and a history of moves, the newest being current. Then he makes several wrong copies by naive random corruption: adding, replacing, removing and shuffling addresses, so each database is wrong in a different way ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 7:39](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=459)). The choice between the two follows from use. Qud's histories are read, so they only need to seem caused; Larsen's are deduced from, so they must be consistent underneath.

### Planning stories

Stephen G. Ware summarises 25 years of story planning. A planner treats events, each roughly one sentence (subject, verb, object), as actions with preconditions and effects that change the world, and searches forward from the initial state through all applicable events until it reaches an ending state. Searching over every event sequence is the most flexible approach and the most expensive; reactive planning looks only one or a few events ahead, and storylets are similar to events but scene-sized ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 4:38](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=278)). World knowledge is stored as variables with values (a character's location, whether they are alive), but Ware says the interesting reasoning lives in metadata about past events and possible futures ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 21:41](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1301)).

He distinguishes two kinds of planner. A *classical* planner needs story context hand-written into preconditions (only rogues steal); in his analogy it puts Lego bricks together any way they fit, so it is up to you that they always look good. A *story* planner lets authors write basic events and infers who acts and why, combining bricks only in ways that make sense, but that requires a formal and complicated model of what makes sense ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 6:33](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=393)). Ware adds that authoring a set of actions with a target story in mind usually yields something totally different and hilariously terrible ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 21:41](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1301)).

The practical limits are real. Planning can require searching billions of sequences, and story planners currently manage about 5 to 10 events at runtime. Ware's group speeds them up with heuristics that sketch the rest of the story, by building only plans whose events enable later events, and by restricting events to the people, places and goals salient in the player's working memory ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 17:01](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1021)). The deeper problem is definitional: formal definitions of story swing between too broad and too narrow, each expansion admitting stories that shouldn't exist and each restriction losing ones that should ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 26:24](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1584)). Large language models do not dissolve this. Ware finds them good at open-ended storytelling but, surprisingly, no better than older heuristic methods at long-term story planning, and hard to make follow a formal story definition, though thinking models and outline-first approaches are improving ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 17:20](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1040)).

### Sifting stories from simulation

Planning makes a story happen; *story sifting* finds stories that have already happened in a simulation. Max Kreminski's Felt expresses sifting patterns as Datalog-style logic queries over event sequences, with clauses that constrain event attributes, shared actors and character traits. His example pattern looks for two betrayals perpetrated by the same character, who has the trait *impulsive*, with a not-join clause excluding certain intervening events ([Max Kreminski 2020, 2:59](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=179)). Patterns are groups of interrelated events that make good narrative building blocks, such as love triangles or revenge cycles, so authors should be able to write many of them quickly for diversity; Felt is built in JavaScript on the DataScript library ([Max Kreminski 2019, 15:14](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=914)).

Writing them quickly turns out to be the hard part. Authors must learn query semantics that behave more like SQL than Python or JavaScript, learn each simulation's own event types and traits, and remember constraints that seem obvious to a human but that the computer cannot infer ([Max Kreminski 2020, 4:09](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=249)). Kreminski's answer is to synthesise patterns from examples. General program synthesis searches a huge, unbounded space and makes the desired behaviour hard to specify; inductive logic programming instead finds a logic program, a Felt pattern, that separates event sequences you want to match from similar ones you don't ([Max Kreminski 2020, 5:19](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=319)). His tool Synthesifter extracts yes/no properties from each positive example (does event three have the tag swing-and-miss? do two events share a batter?) and keeps only the properties shared by all positives, which translate directly into a pattern. Designers first define domain rules, such as what counts as a weak hitter or a pivotal moment in his baseball example ([Max Kreminski 2020, 7:16](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=436)). Earlier, Kreminski had described generating patterns, or replacing them with generic "sifting heuristics" of the kind James Ryan proposed, as unexplored in his lab; he also noted that intern-written patterns made characters see events too similarly ([Max Kreminski 2019, 27:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1661)).

### Checking a story generator by asking it again

Story generators are hard to evaluate from one output. Jasmine Otto's method is to ask for repeated retellings of the same events, or for new stories, and "converse with the deck": the variations tell you whether it is making principled decisions or starting to contradict itself. She notes this works less well in generic story worlds ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 6:15](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=375)). Cook's test scenario for mechanics and Otto's retelling are the same move: when you cannot define quality, build a situation where you will recognise it.

## Seeing what your generator makes: sampling, metrics and expressive range

You cannot tune what you cannot see, and a generator is hard to see. Abdelrahman Madkour says plainly that evaluating whether a generator is any good remains an open research problem; even humans struggle to explain why outputs work ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:04](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=124)). Oliver Withington names three reasons: it is trivial to build a generator with quintillions of unique artifacts, each artifact can be slow to evaluate, and quality is subjective (his own two-person team often disagreed about whether a level was good). There is no universal measure, but trying to understand the space is still worth it ([Oliver Withington 2024, 4:33](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=273)).

### Sampling, and why it misleads

The universal first step is content sampling: generate some artifacts and look at them. One good artifact proves good content exists; one broken one proves broken content exists. Withington's caution is that for a large generative space, even many samples can give a myopic view. Sampling may be enough for tightly constrained generators, such as grammars or cellular automata whose trillions of maps tend to look perceptually similar ([Oliver Withington 2024, 6:30](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=390)). Kate Compton describes the alternative state of affairs: it is really hard to understand the space of what you are generating until you have hit refresh a thousand times ([Kate Compton 2016, 23:22](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1402)).

### Expressive range analysis

The answer the field converges on is expressive range analysis (ERA): generate many outputs, score each on a few metrics, and plot the distribution to see which regions of the design space the generator covers. Madkour credits the idea to Smith and Whitehead, who generated many Mario-style levels, scored each with 0-to-1 metrics such as linearity and leniency, and plotted a heatmap in which darker cells show where more levels fall ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:44](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=164)). A 2018 lightning talk relays the same method from Gillian Smith's essay in *Procedural Generation in Game Design*: define metrics such as density or AI-measured difficulty, generate a thousand levels, and see, for instance, that the generator clusters at mid leniency with either very low or very high linearity ([Various 2018, 2:22](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=142)). Withington describes it identically for Minecraft-like maps (tree coverage, average mountain height), notes it is common in research and used in industry under other names, and says it is most useful when you know what diversity you want, though even without targets it shows what the system can and cannot make ([Oliver Withington 2024, 7:41](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=461)). Three talks across six years describe the same routine, which makes ERA the closest thing to standard practice the talks offer.

> Every piece of content created by the system can be measured and plotted on this n-dimensional generative space. — [Various 2018, 2:22](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=142)

ERA becomes a steering tool when you repeat it across parameter settings. Change parameters such as maximum level size or number of platforms, re-plot, compare, and choose the setting whose output shape best matches what you want ([Various 2018, 3:20](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=200)). Compton credits Gillian Smith and Michael Cook with tools that map output across tuning parameters, for example plotting platformer difficulty against tuning values A and B, so you can watch clusters move and slice off bad regions instead of hitting refresh ([Kate Compton 2016, 23:22](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1402)). Cook's Danesh, a Unity plugin, packages this: visualise the expressive range, click a point to see the level behind it, move sliders to watch the range shift, and run local search to optimise parameters toward a metric ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 6:47](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=407)).

### Choosing metrics

Metrics are proxies, not quality. Madkour is emphatic that they are heavily game-dependent and that you will not get a function that tells you a level is good; pick measurements that matter for your game, such as the number of paths to completion in a dungeon ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 5:04](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=304)). Linearity and leniency are only the canonical example. Number of rooms, number of enemies or how many arms an enemy has are equally valid, and the session's host, Alexei, described building similar visualisations of resource distribution across the map of a AAA survival crafting game ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 27:36](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1656)). Madkour also admits the limit: current metrics are relatively crude and not nuanced enough to capture the design qualities designers care about, and designing better ones is an open question ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 25:02](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1502)).

When you cannot name a good metric, Withington suggests dimensionality reduction. Generated content is effectively a list of values, so, as with correlated variables in a healthcare dataset, you can compress it to two abstract components that explain much of the variance and plot those. The axes are not interpretable, but the plot shows at a glance whether one tuning is more diverse than another, or produces content another generator never would. It works best on small content representations, because these algorithms scale poorly to thousands of variables ([Oliver Withington 2024, 11:30](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=690)).

### Using the plot to choose what to look at

ERA does not replace looking; it tells you where to look. Withington recommends using the visualisation to pick artifacts for hand inspection: the extreme outliers and representatives of each cluster, rather than random samples. Seeing what the generator does when it rolls the equivalent of many sixes in a row tells you whether the extremes are broken or interesting enough to push toward ([Oliver Withington 2024, 12:50](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=770)). The plot also works as pseudo bug-finding. In his toy example, a cluster of maps with 100% water coverage and lots of trees would reveal broken output that even heavy sampling would miss ([Oliver Withington 2024, 8:49](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=529)).

If you are comparing generators, compare fairly. Emily Halina chose comparison levels at random from 100 generated by each approach, so she was not cherry-picking, and turned off Sturgeon's playability constraint because her own method, TRP, has no playability guarantee ([Emily Halina 2024, 19:16](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1156)).

### Enumerating the whole space

Sometimes you do not need to sample at all. Mark Gritter points out that because Rogue uses a 32-bit seed, it can produce only about 4 billion layouts per dungeon level, out of an abstract space of around 10^30; virtually every room configuration you could write down is unreachable ([Mark Gritter 2025, 7:32](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=452)). Enumerating every one turned out to be cheap: he expected to need parallelisation or a GPU, but simply compiling Rogue's generator code ran through all 4 billion seeds in about 11 minutes of CPU time ([Mark Gritter 2025, 7:56](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=476)). His conclusion is that generators with 32-bit seeds can be fully explored, so a developer could check that nothing bad ever happens across every possible seed ([Mark Gritter 2025, 11:11](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=671)).

With the whole space in hand, Gritter post-selected on fixed features, such as the smallest possible upper-left room, and plotted room-occupancy heatmaps and the extremes of total room area. Fixing one room's size showed no gross anomalies. Fixing two exact 4x4 rooms left only 209 seeds, which means a seed can be reconstructed from as few as three room configurations ([Mark Gritter 2025, 9:21](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=561)). He also found that actual Rogue produces fewer very small levels than abstract probability predicts, and is unsure whether that is an artifact of its linear congruential random number generator or just chance; his bet is chance, and dimensionality reduction has not settled it ([Mark Gritter 2025, 9:55](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=595)).

### Small, fast checks against targets

Not every generator needs plots. Elliot Trinidad tuned Blaseball's name pool by repeatedly generating ten names, reading them aloud, and checking them against target ratios per ten: one or two absurd or comedic, five to ten that sound explicitly non-white, nine or ten fun to say, perhaps one tongue twister. When too many were hard to pronounce, he removed, changed or rebalanced entries. He preferred this quick trial and error to writing a tagging program ([Elliot Trinidad 2023, 25:34](https://youtu.be/9yFferxbrBU?t=1534)). What makes it work is the explicit target. Reading ten aloud is sampling, but sampling against stated ratios is a cheap form of measurement.

### Looking at output in context

Statistics show the generator in isolation. Mike Cook argues that is not where its meaning lies. Sample grids, statistics and expressive range histograms are useful, and he uses them every day, but the way people talk about procgen has barely changed since the early 1980s, and he asks what these methods leave out ([Mike Cook 2026, 2:43](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=163)). His thesis, drawn from street photography, is that a generator is best understood not through what it generates but through how its output collides with everything else in the game. Analysing generated content alone is like posing it in a portrait studio; games are tangled webs of systems ([Mike Cook 2026, 23:01](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1381)). A good street photograph needs at least two reasons to be taken: an inflatable location pin over London's South Bank is one reason, two tourists reading a map beneath it a second. Interesting moments come from independent systems colliding ([Mike Cook 2026, 10:01](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=601)).

Isaac Karth's two lenses frame the same choice. You can judge a generator by its individual artifacts, the single snowflake, asking what effect one output has on the player and which differences between outputs matter; or by the impression of its whole generative space, the blizzard, asking what the space feels like overall, whether outputs always or never have some property, and whether connections between them matter ([Isaac Karth 2019, 3:01](https://youtu.be/MHEkE7nPuZc?t=181)). Expressive range analysis is a blizzard tool. Cook's method adds tools at three scales:

- **The city.** Ask how each generator contributes to the overall dream of the game. A whole game is as hard to describe as a whole city; Cook notes that Dwarf Fortress's own store page says it is hard to explain how good its generation is ([Mike Cook 2026, 16:57](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1017)).
- **The street.** Sample your whole game at one location, like a school field quadrant survey. Stand somewhere, such as Joppa in Caves of Qud, and record every system and source of generated content visible from there and which systems are talking to each other. You are sampling the game, not a generator ([Mike Cook 2026, 18:14](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1094)).
- **The lens.** Crop a single object or screenshot and ask what evidence of all your generative systems it shows and what stories it leads the player to. His example is a Dwarf Fortress dwarf description, where you cannot see the fortress or the year but can intuit how generators shaped the dwarf; he credits Florence Smith Nicholls's work on archaeological game design ([Mike Cook 2026, 22:50](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1370)).

Two of his examples double as working habits. Liam Wong's photo *Night City* was made like sampling a generator: he shot one Tokyo intersection repeatedly while systems changed at different speeds (rain and advertising boards in seconds, crowds more slowly, the city over decades), then curated one frame and even re-cropped it afterwards ([Mike Cook 2026, 12:52](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=772)). And when examining your own game, ration yourself: go in with a "roll of 30 photos" and no more, and you will choose more deliberately what is worth capturing ([Mike Cook 2026, 28:40](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1720)).

### A layered routine

The talks do not prescribe a single procedure, but their methods stack naturally into one:

1. **Sample** a handful of outputs to see that good and bad content both exist, and check small samples against explicit targets where you have them, as Trinidad did.
2. **Plot** a large batch on metrics chosen for your game, or on reduced dimensions if you cannot name metrics; re-plot across parameter settings.
3. **Inspect the extremes and the clusters** the plot reveals, treating impossible clusters as bugs. If your seed space is small enough, enumerate it and check every case.
4. **Look in context**: survey one place in the game, crop one screenshot, and ask what the generator's output collides with.

The first three steps tell you what the generator can make. Only the fourth tells you what it means to a player.

## Steering a generator: parameters, optimisation and learning from examples

Seeing a generator's output tells you where it lands. Moving it somewhere else is a separate problem, and the talks offer three answers: expose the right knobs, let an optimiser turn them for you, or show the system examples of what you want and let it learn the weights ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 8:33](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=513); [Aaron Santos 2019, 8:18](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=498); [Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 11:39](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=699)).

### Expose the knobs first

Abdelrahman Madkour's starting principle is to parameterise the generator. Instead of rewriting a hand-built algorithm every time it misses the region of output you want, pull out iteration counts, limits and rule weights so that its expressive range, as plotted in the previous section, becomes something you steer by turning knobs; for a grammar, that means controlling which rules apply or weighting them ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 8:33](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=513)).

Aaron Santos describes what happens when you do not. Generators accumulate magic numbers, values picked until the output looked right, which then interact unpredictably and break when the code or the game's balance changes. He opened the source of NetHack, Crawl, Angband and Pixel Dungeon and found undocumented magic numbers within a minute in each, with the designer's intent hard to recover ([Aaron Santos 2019, 1:37](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=97)).

Santos's refactoring makes the generator a pure function of two things: its parameters and its random input. Pull every magic number out as an explicit parameter, and instead of calling `rand` inside the generator, pass the random values in ([Aaron Santos 2019, 2:35](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=155)). That separation is what makes the next two techniques possible: once output depends only on (parameters, random input), you can score it and search over parameters.

### Route one: optimise against a loss function

Santos borrows the loss function from machine learning. Compute metrics on the generator's output, such as density, connectedness, emptiness or jaggedness, compare each to a target value (squared difference works) and sum; he found these simple metrics worked well for dungeon generation ([Aaron Santos 2019, 3:17](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=197)). Then tune the parameters by mini-batch gradient descent. Santos used jax, a drop-in replacement for numpy that can differentiate suitably structured programs, to get the slope of the loss with respect to each magic number. Start the parameters at tiny random values, evaluate a batch of 32 random inputs, and nudge the parameters along the slope until they converge ([Aaron Santos 2019, 8:18](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=498)). The batch size is a compromise: one example per step gives a wandering descent path, while huge batches are slow to compute ([Aaron Santos 2019, 9:27](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=567)).

The payoff Santos stresses is not the tuned numbers themselves but what the loss function does for the team. Once it finds good values automatically, you can change the generator or its goals without fear and simply re-optimise, and the metrics inside the loss become lasting documentation of what the generator is meant to do ([Aaron Santos 2019, 11:27](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=687)).

> The loss functions with those metrics inside of them are really good ways to document the goals we are embedding. — [Aaron Santos 2019, 11:27](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=687)

The method has a cost. Differentiable programming needs continuous floating-point parameters, and not all code can be made differentiable. Asked how it compares with a genetic algorithm and a fitness function, Santos's tentative impression was that gradient descent is very efficient while genetic algorithms cope better with discontinuity but may optimise more slowly ([Aaron Santos 2019, 13:33](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=813)).

### Route two: learn from examples the designer picks

Madkour argues against handing control to an optimiser. Brute force, hill climbing or genetic algorithms do work, and a small space can simply be brute-forced, but they hide control inside the search method rather than giving the designer a direct handle on the generative space; you end up dependent on designing the optimisation, which is the same difficulty you started with ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 11:12](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=672)). The two positions are less opposed than they look: Santos's loss function is itself a statement of intent, written as metrics; Madkour's objection is to intent that lives only inside the search.

Madkour's alternative is learning from examples. Plot the expressive range, select the outputs in the region you want, mark those parameterisations as good, and let the system shift the generator toward producing more like them ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 11:39](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=699)). His implementation controls a graph grammar by recording each output's generation chain: which applicable rule was picked, and which right-hand side of that rule was used. Probabilities live at both levels, so tracking the choices made for the selected outputs lets the system compute new weights. In his demo you select a region, train on it and see the result ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 22:10](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1330)).

The limit is built in. Reweighting changes how often each output appears, not what the grammar can produce. Madkour calls this double-edged: if the grammar is well formed, levels stay playable, but the adjusted generator can never be more diverse than its base grammar, and it does not escape the oatmeal problem described earlier in this chapter, because that comes from the grammar and the metrics ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 32:58](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1978)). Use reweighting to move within a space you already like; use structural changes to enlarge it.

### Lighter levers

Not every generator needs an optimiser. Emily Halina points out that when generation is near-instant, as in her TRP system, tuning becomes guess-and-check: try values, generate hundreds of levels, look. She found segment size somewhat sensitive per domain (smaller for Zelda, column-sized for Mario) but quick to tune with something like a binary search ([Emily Halina 2024, 16:20](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=980)). And for a pool-based generator the content is the parameter: Sonat Uzun steers Tea Garden's music by editing the small pools from which motifs are drawn, so different pool contents give different motifs and different songs ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 13:55](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=835)).

## Simulated players: solvers, Monte Carlo and tree search as evaluators

Metrics on a map tell you about the map. What a designer usually wants to know is what a player will experience: how hard it is, whether it is consistent, whether it is interesting. A model of the player that actually plays the output can help you assess all three ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 29:02](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1742)). The talks describe three kinds: rule-based solvers, Monte Carlo simulation, and Monte Carlo Tree Search.

### Your puzzle is a secret dungeon

Jack Schlesinger, writing generators for puzzle games including Knotwords, offers a framing that maps cleanly back onto roguelikes: treat a puzzle as a dungeon, where the techniques needed to solve it are the monsters and the order of solving steps is the path through the dungeon. It applies especially to unique-solution, no-guessing puzzles, and his team took many cues from roguelike dungeon generation ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 9:50](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=590)).

Building the solver comes first, and its rules come from people. Play a lot, name the intuitive steps you take, confirm them with statistics over the content, and watch playtesters. In Knotwords an intuition that "EY" almost always appears in that order became a solver technique once frequency analysis over common-word lists showed which letter pairs are ordered one way 90 to 95 per cent of the time; watching where playtesters start, and asking what they think, yields more rules ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 16:43](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1003)).

With a solver in hand, Schlesinger reads three properties off its path:

- **Difficulty.** Score each technique, count them along the solver's path, and run more than one solver. A beginner solver that knows only easy techniques takes a roundabout path; an expert solver shortcuts. Together they tell you how hard the puzzle is for each kind of player. Where no technique catalogue existed, as in Knotwords, they used features instead: letter sets with only one possible ordering are less interesting than those with several valid vowel and consonant positions ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 21:42](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1302)).
- **Interestingness.** Look at how often the same technique repeats ("hidden single, hidden single, hidden single"), whether one dominates, how many different techniques appear, and how different the alternative paths are. For puzzles with guessing, look for spots that are consistently easy or hard versus inconsistent ones ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 26:49](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1609)).
- **Consistency.** Run the solver many times with different seeds and take the population variance of difficulty. High variance means the puzzle is arbitrarily hard or easy depending on the order the player approaches it; Schlesinger wants plenty of difficulty, but not swingy difficulty ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 28:07](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1687)).

droqen converges from the Sudoku side. He uses an off-the-shelf solver both to validate generated puzzles and to grade them by the strategies they require, a list that came free with the solver library, and keeps only puzzles that can be solved without brute force ([droqen 2026, 24:56](https://youtu.be/KfYWVLV5UxQ?t=1496)).

Schlesinger's closing argument turns the framing back on roguelikes: treat a dungeon like a puzzle, and a solver or simple player model can teach you about its difficulty, consistency and interestingness ([Jack Schlesinger 2022, 29:02](https://youtu.be/5PF9RB0_ifM?t=1742)).

### Monte Carlo simulation for balance

Phenry Ewing defines Monte Carlo simulation as modelling a complex game system and sampling it thousands of times with RNG and weighted random variables, to predict outcomes too complex to calculate analytically ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 3:02](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=182)). He defends it against the more elegant alternative: analytical models of complex games tend to simplify away the hardest parts. When an MIT professor proposed an analytical treatment of Werewolf, Ewing asked how he had modelled the seer, the hardest part, and the answer was that he had ignored it ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 16:40](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1000)).

Ewing's warnings are about whether the simulated players resemble real ones. The simulation predicts reality only if the model is fairly accurate, the sample is large enough, and the sampling represents how real players behave: in his pachinko analogy, you drop balls where real players would, not only down the middle or perfectly evenly ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 9:23](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=563)). Treating every free variable as equally likely is unrealistic; feed the model measured player data where you have it, as he did for Cat Burglar, and informed weighted guesses where you do not, as he had to for Werewolf ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 29:37](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1777)). In Q&A he agreed it works best for games with limited player actions, and said that without running thousands of real people through a game, player psychology is guesswork ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 31:22](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1882)).

### Monte Carlo Tree Search

Where Ewing's simulated players follow weighted rules, a tree search lets the simulated player look ahead and choose. Lachlan Kingsford wanted his board game to play itself repeatedly and produce statistics before human testers saw it. He chose Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over machine learning because MCTS is understandable and can be worked through by hand on a whiteboard, where a neural network is a black box of dot products ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 6:10](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=370)).

The heart of MCTS is the upper confidence bound (UCB). Kingsford explains it with four unidentified swords: because hits are random, a great sword may start badly and a bad one may crit, so you try each and favour the better as confidence grows. UCB balances how good an option looks, how sure you are, and how much it has been explored, and at the end you pick the most-visited option ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 7:49](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=469)). The algorithm itself is a four-step loop:

1. **Select:** from the root, recursively take the child with the highest UCB (the lowest on an opponent's turn, since opponents minimise your reward).
2. **Expand** the selected node.
3. **Evaluate** it by simulation.
4. **Propagate** the reward back to the root.

Each node stores N, its visit count, and Q, its average reward. More iterations make it stronger, it performs fairly well even at low counts, and the final move is the child with the highest N ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 10:18](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=618)).

Two adaptations matter for roguelikes. First, randomness: MCTS works best on deterministic games, but chance can be modelled with "game" nodes whose children are sampled by probability weight, such as the distribution of two dice, rather than chosen by UCB. Kingsford adds such nodes for his game's random setup, and notes that while MCTS can show a game is winnable, quantifying how winnable is hard ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 29:05](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1745)). Second, length: chess lasts about 45 moves and Go about 250, but NetHack about 80,000 turns, so random playouts to the end with win/loss rewards teach nothing. Simulate around a thousand turns, score by metrics like health, add intermediate rewards such as approaching the staircase, and cull moves that lose instantly. MCTS optimises exactly what you reward, so reward design is trial and error ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 13:32](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=812)).

Emily Halina, whose TRP generator is driven by an MCTS agent, names the adoption cost from the generator side. You need a hand-designed reward function, which takes expert knowledge and trial and error, and a forward model that can simulate the game's future, which is hard if the game was not built to be simulated; you must also encode what counts as an enemy or a goal state, and running and optimising the search takes time ([Emily Halina 2024, 26:13](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1573)). If you intend to use simulated players, design the game so it can be simulated from the start.

### Real players as the simulation

The last option skips the model. Ezra Szanton proposes building a deckbuilder's synergy network from analytics, measuring win percentage when players hold particular card pairs, to diagnose whether the game behaves as intended. He has not done it yet; he plans to try it in Mr. Magpie's Harmless Card Game, and flags synergies among three or more cards as unexplored ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 25:33](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1533)).

## Generators a team can work with: languages, pipelines and debugging

A generator is used by people: the engineer who wrote it, designers who feed it content, sometimes players or other artists. Whether it is any good in practice depends as much on the environment around the algorithm as on the algorithm.

### Tools that expose the procedure

Spencer Egart argues that generators can be exposed through content-creation tools that give a non-code interface to the generation procedure, usable by non-engineers, by a team, and by the developer. He is careful about "non-code": visual scripting and domain-specific languages are in a way still code; he means not writing code in an IDE ([Spencer Egart 2021, 1:33](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=93)). His node-based pipelines can branch: a "region has room" node sends BSP regions (rectangles from binary space partitioning) that hold a prefab room out one output and empty ones out another, the empty regions get a padded rectangle carved, and everything feeds back into an A* hallway carver ([Spencer Egart 2021, 7:17](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=437)).

### A language is its whole environment

Kate Compton, whose Tracery appeared in the grammar section, argues that a generative language is not its syntax but its environment: the IDE, the error messages, the community, the tools and libraries. Processing understood that bundling an IDE, debugger and compiler mattered more than its Java-variant language ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:26:49](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=5209)). Her tongue-in-cheek test is "Compton completeness": can a first-time user make something expressively significant in an hour, on the device they have, connected to a platform that gives it meaning? Tracery alone is not complete; with editors such as artbot.club or the spiral editor, and with Twitter and Cheap Bots Done Quick, the ecosystem is ([Kate Compton 2020, 19:38](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1178)).

She adds three properties of good generative languages ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:27:31](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=5251)):

- **Scaffolded:** they guide the user toward writing correct programs.
- **Unfoldable:** users start simple and add complexity gradually, as HTML runs from plain text to tags to JavaScript.
- **Little:** they fit politely inside other systems, as regular expressions socket into many languages.

Data format matters too. Compton made Tracery for stories, but because it works on plain text, users bent it to ASCII art, SVG, HTML, emoji and JSON; she took it further with generators that generate generators, such as an art colony of bots with their own SVG styles that critique each other ([Kate Compton 2016, 26:36](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1596)). If you design your data to be flexible, users will find uses you did not plan.

Architecture can simplify in the same spirit. Liza Knipscher started Bioloom with separate methods for plants and animals, then realised her creature generator could make trees. Animals, trees, fungi and each tile of grass now come from one generator; grass is the same kind of organism rendered differently, with its own lifespan and metabolism. The result was simpler code and plant-animal hybrids such as a giraffe with trees and an eyed mushroom on its neck ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 9:50](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=590)).

### Debugging what you cannot see

The danger of data-driven generation is that errors multiply silently. Patrick Kemp, describing design tooling at Spry Fox, warns that procedural config patterns are borderline code-like, complicated and unpredictable: a designer who misunderstands one source config can generate lots of bad content without realising it, and tags can connect things that should not be connected ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 13:50](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=830)). The remedy he wants is a dashboard view that generates many terrains and reports which content is over- or under-used and how often terrain meets the specs gameplay requires ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 23:55](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1435)). Compton shows a related tool, built by two colleagues for a procedural storytelling game, that maps where combinations of game state have high or low ratios of problems so authors can see whether what they wrote actually covers what can arise; she credits this to standardising game logic as data ([Kate Compton 2016, 22:59](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1379)).

At the low-tech end, Mark Johnson debugs Ultima Ratio Regum's riddle generator by running it in isolation thousands of times and manually checking an illustrative subset. He admits it is done with tremendous difficulty and is not perfect ([Mark Johnson 2023, 32:04](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1924)).

### Start from the output

Ada Null built Kiss Garden by first writing out by hand what a desired output should look like, then building simple event generators to reach it; with a target in hand, getting there was not hard ([Ada Null 2025, 11:58](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=718)). A hand-written target output gives the team a shared specification before any code exists, and later a reference to compare samples against.

## Humans in the loop: curation, collaboration and responsibility

The generated content people remember usually had a person choosing it. Several independent talks reach this point from different directions, and it changes how you should think about where the human sits in your pipeline.

### Selection is where quality comes from

Ben Berman says influential computer-generated content usually relies on human curation: impressive examples hide that most of the output may not feel human-made, and reaching a high hit rate without curation is the hard open problem. He concedes that players do accept randomly placed obstacles in popular games and roguelikes ([Ben Berman 2017, 35:16](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2116)). Emilia Lazer-Walker compares comedy Twitter bots to Skinner boxes: most output is oatmeal, and the occasional good result keeps people watching. A bot's author can curate, but a real-time generator like her Computational Flaneur, which responds to live input, cannot; it can only try to choose poems it thinks will interest you ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 19:01](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1141)).

Martin Pichlmair turns this into a recipe. Discussing the cut-up technique, he describes the delightful generative formula as a few rules, plus controlled randomness, plus a human who performs an activity and selects the result. Generators that just hand you results are boring; he finds neural language models boring partly for that reason ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 14:54](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=894)).
Botnik built a tool on exactly that principle: text generation as an instrument, with a human author intervening after every word, rather than a neural net producing a page of output to laugh at ([Botnik 2017, 3:20](https://youtu.be/IujSOW1OMWk?t=200)).

The clearest evidence comes from a game that removed the human. Gabriel Koenig's Test Tube Titans lets players evaluate and select mutations; a late-added auto-mutation used the same process but took one path without player evaluation, and the titans almost always turned out terrible. Koenig likens the player's role to machine learning, random products assessed by trial and error toward a goal ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 13:15](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=795)).

### Players as collaborators

If selection drives quality, the player can be the selector. Koenig contrasts his two games. Jettomero created the illusion of a predetermined world; Test Tube Titans was meant to be the opposite, a chance to go hands-on with the procedural systems and take ownership of a mutation system, which changed his view of generation from a tool to a way of collaborating with players ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 1:04:41](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=3881)). Test Tube Titans kept pulling players back because they had an important role in the creative process, and he urges developers to treat procedural generation as a feature that lets players experiment, not only as a content tool ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 16:00](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=960)). Even in Jettomero, the photo mode mentioned at the start of this chapter let some players spend more time creatively exploring the procedural world than playing the two-to-three-hour game; Koenig concludes exploration of procedural systems mattered most when it offered creative engagement ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 5:42](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=342)).

### The designer's relationship to the generator

For the developer, too, the generator can be a collaborator. Koenig compulsively screenshotted Jettomero's generated spaces and was always excited to see what it would make next ([Gabriel Koenig 2020, 3:48](https://youtu.be/xju91VGh2Ps?t=228)). Alexei Pepers maps the range of attitudes with a set of character classes. The arcane mindset treats generation as a system of rules to master; the divine mindset treats the generator as an external entity that can surprise you, like Darren Grey's "half-wild horse" that he steers but which often goes somewhere unexpected ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 13:09](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=789)). Her druid tends a generator like a bonsai, observing output and pruning unwanted results while it grows; she says this fits evolutionary algorithms best but feels it even with transparent tools like Tracery ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 17:28](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1048)). Her warlock bargains, changing inputs and process until the generator meets them halfway, and her cleric keeps rituals like running a rule twice because it works better; she suspects developers behave like clerics more than they admit ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 16:02](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=962)). Her bard embraces procgen's weirdness instead of hiding it to blend with handcrafted content ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 10:17](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=617)), and her sorcerer uses a generator as a mirror for their own ideas, biases and assumptions ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 9:11](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=551)).

Others describe the same partnership in practice. Atty Vohra uses a generator as a "yes, and" improv partner for the lonely work of D&D session prep: a monster that spawns minions when desperate becomes minions that are specters of the characters' loved ones ([Atty Vohra 2021, 8:13](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=493)). When an output cannot be justified, the curator drops that element and builds on the rest; the generator is a teammate you can say no to ([Atty Vohra 2021, 11:28](https://youtu.be/0ydWz1EvMJs?t=688)). Sonat Uzun was often surprised by Tea Garden's music generator, and a glitch that produced an unintended but excellent song led to the idea of making every aspect, including instruments, a motif ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 11:46](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=706)).

### The hand-crafted counterweight

Nat Alison's defence of hand-crafted Sudoku complicates the generator-first view from the other end. A solver can produce a puzzle that is technically hand-made yet feels procedural: she drew an "@"-shaped whisper-line Sudoku in two minutes, let the tool resolve it, and showed that its small X clues added nothing to the logic and existed only for uniqueness, with no intended solve path ([Nat Alison 2023, 17:29](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1049)). Used well, solvers shortcut bad paths and test combinations while the constructor works out the human logic, steering toward a unique, meaningful path; in one puzzle a solver revealed an odd parity pattern, she worked out why, and built the puzzle around it ([Nat Alison 2023, 17:55](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1075)). Conversely, the Miracle Sudoku and some puzzles by setter Clypeal are essentially computer-generated yet feel hand-crafted, because the value lies in a human discovering that such a constrained puzzle can exist and curating the most beautiful solve path; Clypeal generated combinations with a program and picked the best of four ([Nat Alison 2023, 24:08](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1448)). Construction often feels like discovery rather than creation, setting rules and traversing the space of possible worlds like finding a good Minecraft seed ([Nat Alison 2023, 14:24](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=864)).

Alison's conclusion is that hand-crafted versus procedural is a spectrum, not a binary; what matters is human intent and curation communicating something to other humans ([Nat Alison 2023, 24:43](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1483)). That fits the curation argument above: the question is not whether a machine was involved but whether a person chose what reaches the player, and why.

### Algorithms do not absolve you

Pepers ends on responsibility. Procgen is not the same as randomness, and algorithms are not neutral: generators carry their makers' biases, biased input leads to biased output, and using an algorithm as an intermediary does not absolve a creator of ethical obligations ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 21:14](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1274)).

## Machine learning and large language models

Machine learning entered these talks in two waves: models trained on game levels, and generators trained on the internet. The lessons differ, but both end at the same place as the previous section: keep a human between the model and the player.

### Learning levels from data

Ben Berman frames machine-learning content generation as a trade-off. Methods like character-level recurrent neural networks (char-RNNs) need a lot of data and give only a broad intuition of what matters; methods like NLP grammars work on tiny corpora because a person has specified the rules. Methods that discover what matters from little data do not exist yet ([Ben Berman 2017, 1:04](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=64)). His showcase is Adam Summerville's UCSC research: a char-RNN trained on text representations of Super Mario levels produced plausible, playable levels while knowing nothing about jumping or difficulty, assuming only that later parts of a level relate to earlier ones; Berman notes the shown output was probably curated ([Ben Berman 2017, 10:03](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=603)).

Most of Berman's advice is about encoding:

- **Make it one-dimensional.** Treat a level as a sequence, like a platformer where time moves you forward, and almost every ML tool applies. For 2D games like The Binding of Isaac, express a level as several 1D levels plus a small heuristic tweak ([Ben Berman 2017, 17:36](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1056)).
- **Read in a snake.** Reading tiles in a snaking order instead of the uneven chunks of off-the-shelf code greatly improved the Mario results; Berman speculates it helps the network count runs, such as six sky tiles, before placing something ([Ben Berman 2017, 32:13](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1933)).
- **Encode semantics.** Re-encode tiles as categories such as passable, interactable and reward, and record where categories change. Rare features like coins become learnable, and the same encoding lets you train across games ([Ben Berman 2017, 24:31](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1471)).
- **Denoise as an image.** Noise is the biggest problem: stray blocks break the rules of architecture. Push stray bricks against walls and turn them into bookcases, or tweak one half to mirror the other, removing noise and adding symmetry ([Ben Berman 2017, 26:22](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1582)).
- **Rip your data.** Modding-community tools can extract training data from existing games; Berman succeeded with all five or six he tried, and a model trained on raw hexadecimal Geometry Dash levels produced levels that could be pasted into the game and played ([Ben Berman 2017, 18:39](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1119)).

He also warns that many public char-RNN implementations are subtly broken, such as a Python bug that duplicated array references instead of copies and sat in widely used code for months, so a failed experiment may be the code's fault, not the method's ([Ben Berman 2017, 21:40](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=1300)).

Against this, Emily Halina explains why procedural generation via machine learning stays rare: games have very little training data. An autoencoder trained on two Mario levels outputs mostly sky above and ground below, the most common chunk it has seen. She notes the small models she means use consensual data, a level or two from a designer, and no scraping ([Emily Halina 2024, 4:30](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=270)). Two failure modes recur. Todd Furmanski finds ML output can look right but not function, a perfect-looking marble car that cannot drive, which makes post-hoc work with it tricky ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 24:04](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=1444)). And uncleaned training data leaks: Lazer-Walker's poetry network kept reading out snippets of poetry-book title pages, so walkers heard lists of years, and she says a simple Markov chain would have served as well ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 24:03](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1443)). Pepers offers a consolation for opaque models: even when internals are hard to know, you can still look at the outputs and get a sense of the possibility space ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 26:55](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=1615)).

### Internet-trained generators: the Baltimore Orioles effect

Janelle Shane names the central hazard of models trained on most of the internet. They confuse terms used in more than one context: a generated "cooking blog" mixed black-eyed peas the food with the band, and an article flip-flopped between the Baltimore Orioles baseball team and the bird ([Janelle Shane 2022, 2:46](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=166)). In DALL-E 2, the Orioles become birds surrounded by oranges, because orioles eat orange slices at feeders; adding "baseball team" to the prompt still leaves them in bird land, and she got the team perhaps one time in ten ([Janelle Shane 2022, 9:23](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=563)). Both DALL-E and GPT-3 turn the fossil clam genus Megalodon into a shark-like predator, because the more widely discussed meaning overrides the rarer one; training data reflects human editorialising ([Janelle Shane 2022, 12:54](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=774)).

The same mechanism produces bias. Any generator built on internet data can learn distorted versions of names, ethnicities or groups from wherever they appear online, with results from funny to distressing; Shane cites Robyn Speer's sentiment system, which rated Mexican restaurants negatively despite positive reviews ([Janelle Shane 2022, 15:13](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=913)). This leakage is sneaky and hard to auto-filter, as when a Snickers logo produced sneakers ([Janelle Shane 2022, 16:40](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1000)). Because most leading image generators judge output with the same CLIP model, they share the same failures, and patches like invisibly inserting diversity terms into prompts are opaque, partial fixes ([Janelle Shane 2022, 24:33](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1473)). Opening the model to players adds prompt injection: blocking malicious input with clever prompting is a fool's errand, because your application is only as trustworthy as the model's inclination to follow your prompt over the user's ([Janelle Shane 2022, 28:36](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1716)).

Shane's practical advice comes in two parts. Decide whether to use internet-trained AI before starting a project, and decline to build what would harm even a few people, rather than discovering it at the demo stage when someone types in their own name ([Janelle Shane 2022, 19:29](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1169)). And if you use it, generate and hand-pick ahead of time, for brainstorming, injected randomness or background fill, instead of exposing the generator to player input. The host, Alexei, tied this to the procgen tradition of curation between generator and creator, and Shane agreed AI experimenters could learn from it ([Janelle Shane 2022, 21:25](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1285)).

### Writing with a language model

Robin Sloan's GPT-2 work is a detailed practice for doing exactly that. His rule matches Shane's: it is never responsible to pipe raw output straight to players or readers, since it can produce anything from mildly gross to horrifying; his mailed quests come from his system but are heavily filtered ([Robin Sloan 2019, 11:21](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=681)). His techniques:

- **Fine-tune.** He fine-tuned the internet-pretrained GPT-2 on a small corpus of high fantasy novels for about a week, overwriting its sensibility while keeping its grasp of English ([Robin Sloan 2019, 10:26](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=626)).
- **Ask for a sentence count.** Each prompt mixes his authored text with reader inputs and ends with the number of sentences wanted, a key expressive control that lets him guide the model at every turn instead of receiving pages ([Robin Sloan 2019, 8:30](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=510)).
- **Accumulate context.** He chains prompts without clearing context, so earlier generated sentences build a world state; a "land of the dead" introduced early recurred paragraphs later ([Robin Sloan 2019, 9:51](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=591)).
- **Make sharp turns.** Short authored fragments like "a city known for" or "the Dark Lord truly" inject motion or drama and channel the output; he calls them the most fully authored part of the project ([Robin Sloan 2019, 22:35](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1355)).
- **Hide prompts.** Guidance such as "the world was quiet" is fed to the model but not shown, whispering what kind of scene comes next; he thinks this transfers to other neural nets and probably Markov chains ([Robin Sloan 2019, 26:36](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1596)).
- **Veto and regenerate.** Any block that trips a filter is thrown away and regenerated, which he found easier and cleaner than editing or stitching ([Robin Sloan 2019, 12:16](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=736)).

Sloan also asks the prior question. A generator must earn its place by producing beautiful, surprising, guidable language; interest in a technical trick is not enough, and roguelikes show that an old technology can fire the imagination better than a new one ([Robin Sloan 2019, 28:35](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=1715)).

### Containing the chaos

Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster describe Hidden Door's architecture as containing generative AI's chaos within order: rules, procedural generation and design provide control, while the language model supplies surprise in bounded places. Ordered systems produce emergent results you can trace to causes; generative AI's outputs are unexplainable and grow less coherent the longer it runs ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 19:00](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1140)). Wherever possible they reduce a generative decision to a ranking problem, because picking among options is easier than deciding in a vacuum and allows priorities to change later, and they use precomputed word embeddings, such as a genre-ness score, instead of live generation; this is faster, cheaper and easier to debug ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 23:36](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1416)).

### Who should lead the conversation

Gillian Smith argues that the procedural generation community should lead the public conversation about AI. It can explain generative systems as models, abstractions of reality made by flawed humans, and as media that carry messages and amplify human biases. Roguelike generators are usually treated as a medium, not a replacement for human labour, and this community knows how to design meaningful experiences with generative systems ([Gillian Smith 2026, 1:10:51](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=4251)).

## Found structures: real-world data, mathematics and the other arts

Most generators are built from designer-authored rules and content. A smaller set of talks takes structure from elsewhere: real-world data, existing games, mathematical objects, and practices from music and art. Coleman presents borrowing data as one possible answer to the oatmeal problem ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:37:20](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20240)).

### Data bending

Tyler Coleman borrows "data bending" from glitch art, where you might open an image in Audacity and band-pass filter it: feed real-world data into game systems it was not made for and see what comes out. He urges designers to be creative and weird with their data sources ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:21:08](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=19268)). His method for data-driven generation starts with shape: understand the shape of your input and your output (songs and stock charts are both values over time but fluctuate differently), then what the player needs from it, how to keep the source's flavour, and the worst and best cases. He chose "Mountain King" for a dungeon because its three-act shape with climax and calm suits one, and admits his song dungeons start to look alike because what distinguishes songs is hard to carry over ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:37:20](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20240)).

He is candid about cherry-picking. His Moby Dick world map, with TF-IDF to pick distinctive words for place names, Markov chains for region descriptions and region sizes from chapter lengths, looks perfect because an ocean book suits an ocean map. Run Alice in Wonderland through the same pipeline and you get the same coast and islands with different names, which shows how much comes from the base algorithm ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:36:21](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20181)).
