Test a data-driven generator on inputs that do not flatter it.

Coleman also notes that who chooses the data matters as much as what it says. A designer-chosen source can be sculpted, edited and used to sneak in the designer's taste; player-supplied input shifts creative labour to the player, so that play becomes exploring the algorithm, and designers can plant goal patterns that reward particular combinations ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:39:58](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=20398)).

### Other real-world inputs

Others converge on real-world sources. Max Hawkins's framework for randomising his own life is: make a comprehensive map of the space, sample from it, preferably uniformly at random, commit to the result, and observe what changes ([Max Hawkins 2019, 13:42](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=822)). One app picked random Facebook events from a full city listing and chained them into a schedule with a travelling-salesperson optimisation with time windows, taking him in Berlin from a children's puppet show to a taxi school to a government energy conference ([Max Hawkins 2019, 19:03](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1143)). But a raw corpus can be mostly noise: his list of extracted actions is full of vague or non-actionable items like "meet a certain goal", and he has not found the filter that makes it useful ([Max Hawkins 2019, 24:32](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1472)). Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick's self-generating podcast Neutrinowatch combines pure randomisation, procedural change where each day's output feeds the next, and real-world inputs such as news headlines and planetary movements, as in an astronomy show for a different city each night ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 5:14](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=314)).

Younès Rabii took the most direct route: treat a game's code as DNA and flip random bits in the Pokemon Gold ROM to get a new game. He chose it because a ROM is easy to mutate, its construction makes a mutant likely to stay playable, and he knows it well enough to spot every change ([Younès Rabii 2021, 0:43](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=43)). Naive mutation mostly failed: early attempts did not boot or crashed, and only after tuning where and how much to mutate, over about 200 tries, did he get a game you could play past the first room ([Younès Rabii 2021, 2:22](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=142)).

### Mathematics as found object

Paul Hembree borrows composer Tom Johnson's idea of the "found mathematical object", by analogy with Duchamp's Fountain: Pascal's triangle, the Narayana series, cellular automata or Euclidean rhythms used as structures that provoke further systems built on top. He notes that Narayana lattice paths look like melodic ornaments such as trills, and that Loren Schmidt's Good Night Traffic City used cellular automata for world generation as a provocation for other systems like growing plants ([Paul Hembree 2026, 8:18](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=498)). His worked example is Bjorklund's algorithm, devised in 2004 for particle-accelerator power supplies, which distributes n pulses over m slots as evenly as possible. For 5 pulses in 12 slots, pair each pulse with a following silence, leaving two silences over; then repeatedly group the longer sequences with the leftover shorter ones until no short sequences remain. Results are most interesting when n and m are co-prime ([Paul Hembree 2026, 5:52](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=352)).

Nat Alison asks generator makers to take the mathematician's view as well as the toolmaker's. Developers use fractals or noise because they make a cool picture or a fun world; mathematicians want to know why the model behaves as it does. She suggests prodding your tools: why does a cellular automaton produce interesting results, and what strategy does a deckbuilder run converge on ([Nat Alison 2024, 3:38](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=218))? A 2018 lightning talk drew the mirror image: procgen designers build generators and try to understand their output, while chaos theorists visualise observed systems, as in Robert May's bifurcation diagram, to find the generator behind them ([Various 2018, 7:51](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=471)).

### Lessons from the other arts

Mark Gritter connects procgen to serial art, which starts from a rule or set of axioms and produces every artifact satisfying it, presented together; the work is finished only when no possibilities remain, as in Sol LeWitt's 122 incomplete open cubes ([Mark Gritter 2025, 2:24](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=144)). LeWitt's maxim that "the idea becomes a machine that makes the art" does not mean the artist gives up control, but that they commit to all the consequences of an algorithm ([Mark Gritter 2025, 4:11](https://youtu.be/mtSjgxS-QS4?t=251)). For a designer that is a useful discipline: if you keep a generator, accept what it implies, rather than patching every output you dislike.

Matt Carney borrows Robert Carl's distinction, from a book on Terry Riley's In C, between endogenous analysis of a score's materials and exogenous analysis of a live performance. For roguelikes it separates the generator, its grammar and what it can produce, from the player's subjective encounter with one production ([Matt Carney 2026, 14:19](https://youtu.be/SU-VcmsOvZo?t=859)). Much of this chapter's evaluation work is endogenous; the curation and player-model sections are attempts to reach the exogenous.

Finally, Linas Gabrielaitis offers geological folding, where strata move in place by turning over on themselves, as a possible model for a "deep time" procedurality of layered levels. He presents it as a provocation with a question mark, not a worked mechanic; the host, Alexei, suggested in Q&A that NetHack's bones levels, which fold previous games into future ones, are a kind of proto-folding ([Linas Gabrielaitis 2023, 11:56](https://youtu.be/jvZb9WoIHxo?t=716)).

## Tensions and open questions

**How much variety to aim for.** Tyler Coleman wants systems where the right rolls produce rare, weird outliers, because those are what players talk about ([Tyler Coleman 2024, 23:51](https://youtu.be/C6jR41fZjqM?t=1431)), and Nat Alison counts surprise and joy among the criteria for compelling procedurality ([Nat Alison 2024, 18:23](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=1103)). Ada Null's Kiss Garden deliberately stops at perceptual differentiation, short of uniqueness, because sameness that is visibly not repetition produces the ennui the game is about ([Ada Null 2025, 5:36](https://youtu.be/VzoruhRyvqQ?t=336)). The level of difference is a design choice that follows from the feeling you want, not a ladder every generator should climb.

**Constrain or leave free.** Herbert Wolverson's rule is to check every result ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 24:35](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=1475)), Sébastien "deepnight" Benard holds that a shipped generator must be good every time ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 15:04](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=904)), and Brian Walker never lets a generator block progress ([Brian Walker 2018, 30:04](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1804)). Alexei Pepers reports that Caves of Qud keeps generators unconstrained until a specific harm is proven ([Alexei Pepers 2025, 40:37](https://youtu.be/H5EU9_Gdu94?t=2437)), and Bjarke Alexander Larsen finds unchecked randomness acceptable when players can deal with bad outcomes ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 16:20](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=980)). The choice depends on who pays for a bad output: the player who cannot finish, or a player who can route around it.

**Who controls the terrain.** Noise gives direct, tunable maps but handles transitions between terrain types badly ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 14:22](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=862)); physical simulation gives natural shapes but no lever for the shape you want ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 13:18](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=798); [bleeptrack 2025, 24:38](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=1478)). One of Wolverson's fixes for samey noise is to add simulation in the form of erosion ([Herbert Wolverson 2020, 14:38](https://youtu.be/TlLIOgWYVpI?t=878)); Loren Schmidt's answer is to invert the problem, fixing the shape first and solving for heights ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 15:34](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=934)). Which you pick depends on whether the shape or the process is the thing you need to author.

**When content should exist.** Dwarf Fortress-style histories up front and generating a room or an NPC only when the player meets it remain the two ends of an open question ([Tariq et al. 2016, 2:43](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=163)). Alexander Birke generates each cell on entry, which also rules out wave function collapse for him ([Alexander Birke 2024, 5:36](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=336)); Mark Johnson generates lazily but writes abstract descriptions in advance so clues stay true ([Mark Johnson 2023, 22:10](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1330)); Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans adapt content just in time to how the player is doing ([Sersa Victory and Joris Dormans 2026, 21:48](https://youtu.be/NjIduRLJL7U?t=1308)). The deciding factors are whether the game must refer to things before they exist, and whether it should react to the player.

**Uniform randomness is not the goal, but how far to stray?** Andrew Clifton tolerates small statistical flaws such as modulo bias because he has never seen them matter in play ([Andrew Clifton 2020, 7:32](https://youtu.be/e4b--cyXEsM?t=452)); Nifflas deliberately feeds his music human-invented sequences for their biases ([Nifflas 2025, 14:04](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=844)). Both treat statistical purity as beside the point; they differ on whether bias is merely tolerated or sought out.

**Write your own solver or use one?** Kate Compton warns that teams hand-rolling generate-and-discard systems end up writing a worse constraint solver, and recommends off-the-shelf tools such as answer set programming ([Kate Compton 2016, 21:46](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1306); [Kate Compton 2016, 21:24](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1284)). Dead Cells shipped with its prototype's brute-force room fitter, which takes thousands of tries per level, and players don't care ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 23:56](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1436)). A homemade search is fine when it is fast enough and the constraints are few; the solver pays off as constraints pile up.

**Optimise, or learn from examples?** Aaron Santos tunes generator parameters by gradient descent against a loss function and values the loss as documentation of intent ([Aaron Santos 2019, 8:18](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=498); [Aaron Santos 2019, 11:27](https://youtu.be/TsDIUuEneo4?t=687)). Abdelrahman Madkour argues that optimisers hide control inside the search, and prefers reweighting a grammar toward outputs the designer selects ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 11:12](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=672); [Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 22:10](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1330)), while conceding that reweighting can never add diversity ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 32:58](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1978)). Both want the designer's intent explicit; they differ on whether it is better written as metrics or shown as examples.

**Simulate a history, or rationalise one?** Jason Grinblat picks Qud's historical events at random and invents causes afterwards ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 19:14](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=1154)); Larsen simulates a ground truth because his players must deduce from it ([Bjarke Alexander Larsen 2026, 7:39](https://youtu.be/gxXZRofE5dI?t=459)). The answer depends on whether the history is read or reasoned about.

**Statistics or context?** Expressive range analysis judges a generator by its distribution of outputs ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:44](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=164); [Oliver Withington 2024, 7:41](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=461)); Mike Cook argues that a generator's meaning lies in how its output collides with the game's other systems, which statistics in isolation cannot show ([Mike Cook 2026, 23:01](https://youtu.be/nOGNdrjm8ek?t=1381)). They answer different questions: what the generator can make, and what it means to a player.

**Curation where curation is impossible.** Ben Berman, Martin Pichlmair and Nat Alison place quality in human selection ([Ben Berman 2017, 35:16](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2116); [Martin Pichlmair 2026, 14:54](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=894); [Nat Alison 2023, 24:43](https://youtu.be/rcIVCrddozQ?t=1483)), but Emilia Lazer-Walker points out that a real-time generator cannot curate ([Emilia Lazer-Walker 2017, 19:01](https://youtu.be/MNEG1sLSRcM?t=1141)), which is the position of any generator running during play. Berman concedes that players do accept randomly placed obstacles, and calls reaching a high hit rate without curation the hard open problem ([Ben Berman 2017, 35:16](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=2116)).

**What language models are good for.** Stephen G. Ware finds them good at open-ended storytelling but no better than older heuristic methods at long-term story planning ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 17:20](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1040)). Janelle Shane would generate and hand-pick output ahead of time rather than expose a generator to player input ([Janelle Shane 2022, 21:25](https://youtu.be/VhUh9rksfaE?t=1285)), and Robin Sloan says never to pipe raw output to players ([Robin Sloan 2019, 11:21](https://youtu.be/cIpErjWBqm0?t=681)); Hidden Door does run a model live, but contains it within rules and turns its decisions into rankings wherever possible ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 19:00](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1140); [Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 23:36](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1416)). The question is less whether to use one than where the boundary around it sits.

**Unsolved problems.** Evaluating generators is an open research problem, and current metrics are too crude to capture what designers care about ([Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 2:04](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=124); [Abdelrahman Madkour 2022, 25:02](https://youtu.be/_s-Tn0biyEk?t=1502)). Global properties such as symmetry resist local rules ([Ian Holmes 2017, 17:52](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=1072)), and TRP is expected to struggle on logic-heavy puzzles like Sokoban ([Emily Halina 2024, 24:33](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1473)). Formal definitions of story are always too broad or too narrow ([Stephen G. Ware 2025, 26:24](https://youtu.be/Rs_-yMsJDq8?t=1584)), and generic sifting heuristics remain unexplored ([Max Kreminski 2019, 27:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=1661)). Learning levels from little data is not yet possible ([Ben Berman 2017, 1:04](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=64)). Analytics-built synergy networks of three or more cards ([Ezra Szanton 2025, 25:33](https://youtu.be/JfNeYtH7xI4?t=1533)), a filter that turns a noisy real-world corpus into usable actions ([Max Hawkins 2019, 24:32](https://youtu.be/anwk8b7c_s0?t=1472)) and geological folding as a model for layered levels ([Linas Gabrielaitis 2023, 11:56](https://youtu.be/jvZb9WoIHxo?t=716)) are all proposed but untried.

## Checklist

- What should this generator do to the player, and would a hand-made version give a once-through player the same experience?
- Where in play will the player perceive the difference between two outputs, and which level of difference are you aiming for?
- What design knowledge does the generator need, and have you budgeted the time to encode and tune it?
- Are your random rolls shaped by weights, curves or causal links, or are they flat?
- Can you regenerate any location, in any order, from a seed, and reproduce a player's bug exactly?
- When is each piece of content generated, and can the game refer to things that do not exist yet?
- Which global properties (progression, solvability, large-scale order) does your method not see, and what supplies them?
- Which failures block progress, and does an algorithm check for each of them on every output?
- If you patch a failed output in place, are you sure every invariant still holds, or would regenerating be safer?
- Are you writing a constraint solver by accident, and would an off-the-shelf one do the job?
- Have you plotted a large batch of outputs on metrics that matter for your game, and looked at the outliers and clusters by hand?
- Have you looked at the output in context: one place in the game, one screenshot, what it collides with?
- Can a solver or simulated player measure the difficulty and consistency of what you generate?
- Are the generator's magic numbers explicit parameters with documented targets?
- Who selects what reaches the player: you, a curator, the player, or nobody? If nobody, what keeps raw output in bounds?
